items.body: The reason I like John Coltrane’s Concert in Japan best out of all my Coltrane albums is that it includes one of my all-time favorite tracks: “Peace on Earth”. And as good as “Meditation/Leo (Part One),” “Leo (Part Two),” and “Part Three” are - “Peace on Earth” outshines them all. When John Coltrane arrived in Japan in 1966, he was welcomed like a king. He arrived at Haneda Airport on July 8, 1966, along with his wife Alice, Pharoah Sanders, Jimmy Garrison, and Rashied Ali. Ali, who later recalled the trip, said they were greeted by thousands of Japanese fans. At the airport, there were huge, life-size cardboard cutouts of the musicians, a red carpet leading from the plane to the terminal, and bouquets of flowers. And Coltrane had a message, it was no coincidence that he wanted to perform in Japan. He insisted on traveling to Nagasaki to visit the Peace Memorial at the site of the atomic bombing. He laid down a wreath and prayed for a long time. The place had a profound emotional and spiritual impact on him. On the evening of his concert in Nagasaki, he played “Peace on Earth” - at that time a new piece and a kind of musical prayer for peace. At a press conference during the tour, when asked about the Vietnam War, he said: “I dislike war, period. It should stop, and any other war.” On Concert in Japan - and on “Peace on Earth” in particular - one can see how Coltrane’s thirst for new sounds is inextricably linked to his desire to view the universe from a spiritual perspective; his music radiates a cosmic aura. The piece begins with an incredibly beautiful melody that floats above Alice’s arpeggios, Garrison’s bass sprinklings, and Ali’s sparse drumming. It seems like the musical embodiment of the Garden of Eden. Nearly six minutes of pure harmony - but then deliberate atonality creeps in, paradise is threatened, only heavenly saxophone lines save it for the time being. Then, however, a dissonant storm is conjured up, shaking this world to its very foundations. The piece is thrown into utter disarray; block chords replace the arpeggios, and the bass and drums throw the meter overboard. At the very end, however, harmony returns, and the melodies resurface, albeit different from how they began. In July 1966, John Coltrane was just one year away from his untimely death, yet his zest for life was greater than ever. His musical explorations were more adventurous than before, and “Peace on Earth” brilliantly captures the essence of what his music is all about. Or, as my friend Thomas Weber puts it: “On the one hand, it’s utter extravagance and exhaustion, on the other, it’s the dissolution of boundaries. Free jazz with melodies.” Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._genre: free jazz / spiritual jazz / avant-garde / improvisation
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑记录了1966年John Coltrane在日本巡演的现场录音，尤其聚焦于曲目《Peace on Earth》。Coltrane在抵达日本后专程前往长崎和平纪念公园献花祈祷，作品本身也被视为一种音乐层面的和平祈愿。乐曲起始阶段由Alice Coltrane的琶音、Garrison的低音点缀与Ali的稀疏鼓点构成，旋律漂浮其上，营造出近乎伊甸园般的和谐氛围；约六分钟后，不协和音逐渐侵入，节奏被推翻，萨克斯线条在混乱中维系张力；终末时和声重新浮现，但形态已不同于开端。整张专辑体现了Coltrane晚期对宇宙性与精神性视角的追求，声音探索极为大胆，充满即兴张力与结构性破坏，与学院派自由爵士及前卫即兴高度契合。

items.excerpt: wave_function ultimately displays an artist working in top form, mapping out a series of experimental electronic terrains that converge into something uniformly disjointed, immersive, and quietly mind-bending. items.body: wave_function ultimately displays an artist working in top form, mapping out a series of experimental electronic terrains that converge into something uniformly disjointed, immersive, and quietly mind-bending. Broken sonic relics, elastic and stretched to their limits wave_function by Marco Simioni   One of our favorite mechanized glitch-electronic artists, Marco Simioni, returns with wave_function for Barcelona-based Evel, an imprint that continues pushing fractured, futuristic sound-scrapes from artists across the planet. Simioni digs miles and miles into erratic, densely packed rhythmic DSP-laden structures, shaping minimalist extrusions that echo, bend, and arch. Opener “et II no pt re” feels as though its pulsing tone and abrasive grit could push straight through the cosmos. Corrupted sonic data, indeed. Simioni works in infinitesimal layers, carefully weaving hypnotic electro-glitch hybrids into shifting forms and textures. Tracks like “yttr flux” and “vinh 49” emerge as broken sonic relics, elastic and stretched to their limits, while “pulse array for dissolving realities (dive mix)” moves through a restrained ambient propulsion, industrial drone filaments threading through the mix like fragments of an unknown message waiting to be deciphered. “ekkot vire” pushes deeper into abstract electronic substructures, constantly expanding, collapsing, and reforming, before “509dualech2211eren” loops through a haze of ambient flutter, surrounding the listener with microscopic details of tone, drone, and white noise. The ending highlights Simioni’s ability to cultivate tiny, ethereal sound forms that remain ruptured at their edges while maintaining the pulse of a living machine. wave_function ultimately displays an artist working in top form, mapping out a series of experimental electronic terrains that converge into something uniformly disjointed, immersive, and quietly mind-bending. elseq fans should take immediate notice. wave_function is available on Evel. [Bandcamp] wave_function by Marco SimioniThe post Marco Simioni :: wave_function (Evel) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._genre: experimental electronic / glitch / ambient drone / industrial / abstract
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由意大利电子音乐人 Marco Simioni 在巴塞罗那独立厂牌 Evel 发行，是其实验电子创作的一次集中展示。作品以密集的 DSP 编程节奏结构为骨架，在极简的外延音型中塑造不断回响、弯折、弧线运动的声音形态。评论者将多首曲目形容为被拉伸至极限的碎裂声音遗骸，质感充满腐蚀性的数字噪音与失真颗粒；另一些段落则沉入环境推力与工业无人机丝线之中，如同等待破译的未知讯息碎片。终曲以微观级的氛围颤动收束，在白噪音与持续的脉冲中维持着活体机械般的律动。整体呈现出碎片化、沉浸式且安静地扭曲感知的听觉体验，对前卫电子与 IDM 听众具有较强吸引力。

items.body:
This New World CD is by my count the fourth or fifth edition in half a century of a record that should never go out of print. Julius Hemphill released it on LP soon after its 1972 recording on his Mbari label. (Its name is writ large on the original cover; his own name did not appear. New World adds it to the facsimile cover.) He distributed it himself, and not many copies circulated. The album came out to a larger world with the 1977 version in Arista/Freedom’s new music series, with a new and striking cubistic photo-montage cover by Dennis Pohl, and liner notes by Robert Palmer which told us a bit about the West African Dogon people, and about Fort Worth–reared St. Louis–seasoned Hemphill. Curiously Palmer never IDs the backbones of Hemphill’s backbeat, cellist Abdul Wadud and ex-Paul Butterfield, ex-Art Ensemble of Chicago drummer Philip Wilson. (He did mention Julius’ right hand, trumpeter Baikida Carroll.) Advance word of a sort had come the previous year, with the release of Hemphill’s Arista/Freedom Coon Bid’ness, mostly recorded in 1975. It included “The Hard Blues” left over from the 1972 session, a tune which added Hamiet Bluiett’s bari to the core tet. A 2011 (pricey) limited edition CD miniaturizing the Pohl/Palmer package was produced by International Phonograph’s late Jonathan Horwich, who remastered the program from the original tapes, sensibly tacking on “The Hard Blues” as a bonus track. So does the New World version, which also sports new notes by Hemphill colleague/scholar/archivist Marty Ehrlich. The sound has been newly refurbished by Paul Zinman, cleaning up the raggedy/degraded tape ending of “Rites.” (I haven’t seen it, but there’s also a new Superior Viaduct LP edition of the original program/artwork, with notes by John Corbett.)

Wadud’s cello voice is prominent on Coon Bid’ness’ choogling “Skin 1” and “Skin 2,” but even with that album to whet a new Hemphill fan’s appetite, Abdul’s entrance at the top of Dogon’s 15-minute opening/title track was a stunner. First time I heard it, 49 years ago, I fell in love with the album before Julius had sounded a note: Wadud’s grinding one-bar bowed-dyads ostinato turned cello into a big Delta blues guitar. Wadud wasn’t the first jazz cello player by a long shot, though earlier ones mostly treated it like a baby bass. Other improvising cellists cropped up in the 1970s – Diedre Murray, David Eyges, Tristan Honsinger, Tom Cora, Ernst Reijseger ... – with many more soon to come, but nobody brought earthy sensibility and downhome funk to intonation and frictive bowing like Wadud. “Dogon”’s grinder riff nestled in the cracks in Philip Wilson’s sparse 11/16 drums and cymbal tattoo (a 4+4+3 he found tricky to master and held onto, tight, for most of it). And then come the horns, alto and trumpet melded in unison, and occasional blue minor harmony, phrasing like a single entity – the yoked horns of World Saxophone Quartet coming. (WSQ was already active when Arista/Freedom’s Dogon came out.) That melody is a series of bluesy aphoristic phrases that build on what’s already unfolded, then atomizes into a series of exclamatory single notes. The overall structure mirrors that odd-meter bar: the main melody’s sections are 19, 11 and 13 bars long.) In practice the melody seems capable of infinite development, while leaving space for cello and drums to speak through. (The cello part’s built-in variations may outline the harmony, arco or pizz.) And then comes Hemphill’s alto solo over vamping. Ornette’s North Texas holler is somewhere in the distance behind it, but Julius’s tone is dryer and harsher, his blues-infused intonation more sour and pitiless, his wildly scouring line informed by the written material: it’s all of a piece. He boils over and keeps boiling. (Baikida eases into his spot – won’t compete with that.) The blues gets dehydrated and reconstituted.

“Dogon A.D.” is all slow build; swifter “Rites” plunges right into the twisty melody; we’re in the thick of action from the opening seconds, fast but with no fixed tempo, its recurring hook (and opening) a couldn’t-be-simpler drop of a whole step. Thick is right: three-part harmony with cello as third horn, or sometimes as droning tambura. (If Ornette’s in there, it’s the roiling Crisis.) Baikida is especially effective darting behind Julius, blowing bugler’s commentary, reinforcing but never upstaging the boss’ alto. “Rites” is all coiled energy; when it flags, return to the head for a quick exit. For still more contrast, there’s the slowly unwinding “The Painter” for Hemphill’s bucolic sung-multiphonics flute (refreshingly un-Rahsaan-like), its melody both wide-ranging and sing-song catchy. Timing and articulation can be tricky – it’s not a line a part-time flutist writes for an easy layup. Wadud strums or picks rhythm; Wilson rustles; Carroll is as ever the loyal supporter, nimbly selfless, has chops to burn but keeps them in check. It’s the composer’s show, even without Hemphill’s name on the original cover.

And then “The Hard Blues” with its stompy riffy head, looking directly ahead to (and featuring half of) WSQ, but also – with its achingly-slow-to-quick tempos and dense-to-lean textures, suite-like variety and scored interludes – to Henry Threadgill’s 1980s Sextett. Whatever else he did, Julius Hemphill (like other members of St. Louis’s BAG co-op) brought convincing funk to new acoustic jazz, and reaffirmed the blues as eternal wellspring. Timeless tunes, an original group sound, liberatory cello – their appeal does not wear thin. Ehrlich’s notes describe in detail a private video of an earlier performance of the “Dogon A.D.” suite including a first unrecorded movement. The quartet was Hemphill, Carroll, Wilson and pre-Wadud pianist John Hicks, on vibes, playing what I’ve always thought of as the idiosyncratic ‘cello part.’ I imagine this performance as something from an alternate universe, one where Hemphill never performed at Oberlin College in 1970, and never met and jammed with the cellist known to classical audiences as Ronald DeVaughn, and that earthy blue arco scrape never got to shake us to the core.

Ideally Dogon A.D. and Coon Bid’ness should be reissued together, a definitive picture of Hemphill’s (and Wadud’s) music in early bloom. Rights to both are currently held by Germany’s DA Music. But both together are just too long to fit on a single CD. (With thanks to Marty Ehrlich for fielding various questions.)
items.label: New World 80850-2
items._cn_summary: 本文回顾了Julius Hemphill 1972年录制的Dogon A.D.专辑多次再版的历史脉络，指出原版由Hemphill自资发行、印量极少，后经Arista/Freedom进入更广视野。乐评聚焦开篇15分钟同名曲中大提琴手Abdul Wadud的弓奏双音持续音型，将大提琴化作粗粝的三角洲布鲁斯吉他，与鼓手Philip Wilson稀疏的11/16拍击交织；Hemphill的中音萨克斯与小号Baikida Carroll在齐奏中融为单一声音实体，预告了后来的World Saxophone Quartet。文章追溯了1970年代即兴大提琴家谱系（Wadud、Murray、Honsinger、Cora等），认为Wadud在摩擦弓法与本土放克感上的贡献无人可比。Dogon之名与西非多贡族的关联亦贯穿全篇，体现出非裔自由爵士对西非文化根源的呼应。

items.body:
Over the course of the last decade, the group أحمد [Ahmed] has carved out a distinctive approach to the jazz canon through their tireless exploration of the music of Ahmed Abdul-Malik. Mining Abdul-Malik’s compositions and his incorporation of non-Western microtonality into the jazz vocabulary, pianist Pat Thomas, alto saxophone player Seymour Wright, bassist Joel Grip, and drummer Antonin Gerbal have done more than reinterpretation. They have used the music as a foundation for both immersion and subversion of the way that the standard jazz quartet functions within post-bop structures. For last year’s Sama'a (Audition), they went into the studio for an expansive refraction of Abdul-Malik’s Jazz Sahara. During that same session, the four took a slight detour to record Play Monk, a dive into deconstructions of six pieces by Thelonious Monk, all but one of which he recorded in the late 1950s when Abdul-Malik was part of his group. أحمد [Ahmed] has incorporated Monk tunes into their live sets but this is the first time they have focused on his tunes on a recording.

While Thomas, Wright, Grip, and Gerbal have not altered their strategies in the switch of source material, there is one significant shift in the way one listens to this music. A quick search returns no other versions of Abdul-Malik’s pieces other than those recorded by the composer or أحمد [Ahmed] whereas Monk’s “Epistrophy” or “’Round Midnight” have hundreds. Even a less well-known piece like “Oska T” has dozens. Because the pieces covered are so well known, their teasing apart and restructuring of the underlying thematic kernels are more readily evident. Over two CDs, the quartet digs in, with improvisations that range between 20 and 30 minutes with the exception of a seven-minute extrapolation of “Epistrophy.” These extended explorations allow the group to excavate the forms with a focused patience, zeroing in on and elucidating microscopic details, extricating them into the fundamental elements of penetrating improvisations.

The first phrases of the opening “Bye-ya / Epistrophy” provide a glimpse of what is to come. Bass and piano circle around the theme and Gerbal’s lithe drumming circles up to drive momentum. Wright’s stabbing alto picks apart the melody and the four launch off on a circuitous inquiry, dismantling Monk’s tune into its constituent fragments and then reassembling them with constructivist abstraction. Each of the four seize on elements of the underlying piece, playing them off of each other with unwavering resolve, an approach the group continues to advance in their sweeping live sets. There is an insistent intensity as Wright’s notes pick and prod at Thomas’ skewed clusters, Grip’s free walking lines, and Gerbal’s churning free rhythms. Shards of “Epistrophy” are introduced into the mix by Grip and Thomas, slowly accruing with multifaceted erudition.

The group continues to subvert expectations with “Friday the Thirteenth” as Thomas insistently repeats the first phrase of the tune against Grip’s growling arco inversions. Wright’s keypad pops and Gerbal’s open percussion build momentum and Wright unleashes spattered honks that open into a collective four-part splintering of the theme, picking it apart and recasting it with angular exactitude, building density and intensity over the course of the sweeping 26-minute improvisation. “’Round Midnight” gets a relatively straightforward introduction with Wright intoning the theme over sinuous bass and cymbal splashes. Thomas’ spare chords enter as the quartet dynamically transposes the constituent parts of the piece with imperturbable resolution resolving with the riveting cycling hushed snare abrasions that brings the piece to a close.

A seven-minute scorching, stuttering run through “Epistrophy” serves as an interlude to an abstracted, cascading reading of “Evidence” which takes Monk’s stop-start theme and explodes it with relentless, spiraled piano phrases and the hurtling momentum of bass and drums driving Wright’s coruscating alto which prods and jabs with spiky dexterity. The 30-minute improvisation is an engulfing exemplification of unflagging invention. Monk’s “Oska T.,” structured around an obsessively cyclical riff, is a fitting conclusion to the release. The quartet slows things down to a free shuffle with bass and alto arcing over the mutable pulse of piano and drums. The four players adroitly weave their lines in and out of the collective undercurrent with indefatigable ingenuity. While others have dedicated themselves to the reinterpretation of the music of Thelonious Monk, أحمد [Ahmed]’s Play Monk is distinctive in its mastery, fully absorbing his music into the collective rigor and artistry of this singular ensemble.
items.label: Otoroku ROKU047
items._cn_summary: 这支伦敦即兴乐团延续了对Ahmed Abdul-Malik作品的深层探索，此次将焦点转向Thelonious Monk的六首曲目。每首作品均展开为二十分钟以上的长篇即兴，通过解构旋律主题、剥离和声骨架，在后波普框架内进行系统性颠覆。四位乐手以显微镜般的耐心挖掘曲式碎片，钢琴的非传统音簇、萨克斯的尖锐刺探、低音的自由行走线与鼓手的混沌节奏相互碰撞，将熟悉的Monk旋律拆解为基本元素后再以建构主义方式重组。作品展现出对传统爵士四重奏结构的彻底质疑与重塑，是一次对经典曲目在即兴语境下的深度解构实验。

items.album: [2View] Maps and Diagrams’ beneath still stars (handstitched*) & returning light (Home Normal)
items.excerpt: Two decades removed from the clockwork IDM of Polytuft-Tech, Tim Martin’s returning light (Home Normal) and beneath still stars (handstitched*) find him stripping everything back to drift, texture, and quietly resonant melody, resulting in two companion albums that feel less like separate releases than different sides of the same long, unhurried thought.   Companion pieces, two sides of the same drift beneath still stars by maps and diagrams returning light by maps and diagrams   Tim M
items.body: Two decades removed from the clockwork IDM of Polytuft-Tech, Tim Martin’s returning light (Home Normal) and beneath still stars (handstitched*) find him stripping everything back to drift, texture, and quietly resonant melody, resulting in two companion albums that feel less like separate releases than different sides of the same long, unhurried thought.   Companion pieces, two sides of the same drift beneath still stars by maps and diagrams returning light by maps and diagrams   Tim Martin has been Maps and Diagrams since the early 2000s, and the entry point for a lot of people into his catalog is Polytuft-Tech, released in 2003 on Expanding Records, an album that got filed under IDM, ambient, and glitch at a moment when those three words together still meant something specific and rigorous. That record ran on clicky drums that whirred like clockwork under warm, streamlined melodies. It landed near the tail end of IDM’s most experimentally saturated period, right as the genre itself was quietly transitioning into whatever came next, and it stands as one of the more melodically generous statements from that stretch. Both returning light (Home Normal) and beneath still stars (handstitched*) are nowhere near that record sonically. Drums are gone almost entirely. Glitch has been replaced by drift. But it’s still unmistakably Tim, the same restrained, resonant signature that’s followed him through two decades of output, just aged into something quieter. Both albums arrive within weeks of each other on different labels with different histories attached. returning light is Home Normal‘s second release from Tim this year, following tone isolation, his actual debut on the label despite Home Normal running for over seventeen years, a gap explained by the fact that Tim‘s earliest UK work went through Nomadic Kids Republic, Home Normal‘s sister label, back in 2011 with Lights Will Call On You and The Town Beneath The Sea. beneath still stars comes out on handstitched*, the label Tim runs himself, which has carried his more private and experimental output for years alongside releases like In Circles. One album through someone else’s curatorial lens, one through his own. That distinction matters more than it initially seems to. Ambient releases should never get judged track by track in isolation. The genre works as a collective experience, an album like this either builds a sustained emotional environment across its runtime or it doesn’t, and no individual piece can really save or sink that outcome on its own. What matters more is whether the melodies that surface actually resonate, whether they invoke something specific rather than just occupying space. Both of these records succeed at that, though they do it through slightly different means. “ArcWorld-6.4 Rev.42 [sgl.break]” from beneath still stars is one of the more fascinating pieces across either release, another example of the part A / part B structure that’s shown up in other reviews recently. It connects two ideas without part B ever feeling like a continuation of part A. Instead it functions as an introduction to something entirely different, and the transition is peaceful in a way that most of this album is. The track titles throughout beneath still stars read almost like technical drafts, numbered revisions, hertz values, file extensions in brackets like [static] or [lost.wav] or [mem.void]. That naming isn’t arbitrary. It reads like an iteration system, drafts selected and refined specifically rather than titled decoratively after the fact. “Raddius.ocean-IX [r.36-04hz]” is another two-part piece, but this one connects rather than diverges, a drone-like melodic note giving way to a dreamlike synth tuned to a specific frequency, which the title tells you outright. Intentional down to the hertz. “beneath still stars and returning light aren’t competing statements, they’re companion pieces, two sides of the same drift, released close enough together that they start to feel like one long, unhurried thought that just happened to get split across two labels.” ~J. Batista A different level of drone entirely :: returning light sits in the same emotional register but sounds noticeably different sonically. There are small clicks and glitches scattered through certain tracks, and the pads and atmospheres carry a different weight than what’s happening on beneath still stars. “falling rainbows” uses static hits inside its pad environments to create reverbed textures that read almost like snare hits, except Tim‘s building that rhythmic tension entirely out of pad effects and reverb rather than anything resembling a drum sample. “just moving” introduces keys that sound almost like distortion at first before resolving into something prettier the longer you sit with it, a different level of drone entirely, since nothing here holds on a single note. There’s room for other melodies to form and enter, and they do. “somewhat virtual interactions” is a favorite, what sounds like a distorted “ahhh” vocal fragment sits so subtly in the mix that it changes the character of the pads around it, and there are field recording glitches scattered throughout that open up real space inside the track. “Open Water” plays almost like an audio representation of a shishi-odoshi—that traditional Japanese bamboo water fountain that fills, tips, empties, and resets in a slow repeating cycle. Tim‘s using effects here the same way that device uses gravity and water, building a soft, cyclical sense of rhythm entirely out of texture rather than percussion. “ouvertures” closes the album starting soft and distorted, and around the 3:55 mark a low humming frequency starts creeping in that sounds baked into the synth itself, eventually rolling and degrading the audio as the track winds down. A genuinely cool effect to end on. “Tim Martin has landed somewhere his younger self probably wasn’t building toward. Whether that’s evolution or just where two decades of making ambient music eventually deposits a person is hard to say, and probably doesn’t matter.” ~J. Batista There’s a version of this review that picks a favorite between the two records. That version would be missing the point entirely. beneath still stars and returning light aren’t competing statements, they’re companion pieces, two sides of the same drift, released close enough together that they start to feel like one long, unhurried thought that just happened to get split across two labels. beneath still stars is the more clinical of the pair. Drafted, revised, numbered like lab notes, every track title reading like a version history for a synth that never stops evolving. Twenty years removed from Polytuft-Tech‘s clockwork drums and whirring percussion, Tim Martin has landed somewhere his younger self probably wasn’t building toward. Whether that’s evolution or just where two decades of making ambient music eventually deposits a person is hard to say, and probably doesn’t matter. These two records don’t argue for themselves. They don’t need to. They just sit there, patiently, until you notice forty minutes have passed and you’ve barely moved. Home Normal got the warmer half. handstitched*—Tim‘s own label, his own house, got the rawer, more exacting one. He gets to have it both ways. So does anyone who sits with both records long enough to stop telling them apart. beneath still stars is available on handstitched* and returing light is available on Home Normal. beneath still stars by maps and diagrams returning light by maps and diagramsThe post [2View] Maps and Diagrams’ beneath still stars (handstitched*) & returning light (Home Normal) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._cn_summary: 乐评聚焦于Tim Martin以Maps and Diagrams之名在二十年后推出的两张配套氛围专辑：returning light由Home Normal发行，beneath still stars则出自他自己主理的handstitched*厂牌。评论追溯了他从2003年Expanding Records时期精密如钟表的IDM/碎拍风格一路走向剥离节奏、只剩漂浮质感的漫长演化轨迹，凸显其克制而持久的个人音色签名如何在不同策展语境下呈现出不同的情感层次。文章反对逐曲评判氛围作品，强调专辑整体应营造持续的情绪空间，唯有真正引发回响的旋律才有意义。两张唱片分别通过独立厂牌的策展视角与艺术家自我审视达成各自目的，构成同一缓慢思绪的两面。评论信息量充足但内容在末段被截断。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — When I first heard a few tracks by this Finnish band, I gradually realized that what captivated me was the blend of King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard's irreverence toward musical genres, an approach that, while experimenting with them all, still respects them and follows their rules. I was also reminded of The Cardigans: a mix of tradition and the past, combined with a freshness where technology, jazz, and a unique brand of pop came together. Their debut album opens on a serious note with classical piano and violins, key elements of their sound, and the magical voice of Eeva Rajakangas; on the track "T�nne saakka ei aurinko paista," she recites the lyrics, creating a powerful and truly special moment. Kadenssi reveals the strong influence of Nordic traditional music, austere, profound, and almost sacred, and Celtic music, danceable and luminous, sharing a common thread in that both border on the mystical.With the fourth track, Kahdeksas p�iv�, rock and modernity enter the mix, while maintaining that distinctive nine-piece lineup, featuring two violins and a saxophone, where the true fusion begins. A folk atmosphere, driven by the flute, occasionally evokes the folk-rock sound of Jethro Tull; yet, modern drum loops and Eeva's spoken-word vocals merge into a blend of jazz, funk, and punk. Add to this a dissonant chorus and a distorted, psychedelic cabaret vibe, and it feels as though we are witnessing a whole new album within the album itself."Planeetta" plays with space and silence; Eeva's voice sings and then recedes, as does the piano, eventually revealing a jazz-infused atmosphere driven by violins and saxophone, lending the track a distinctive character. It then returns to Celtic roots, yet approaches them not in the traditional manner, but with a rock and funk sensibility, featuring a syncopated, irregular rhythm."08" continues with the distinctly postmodern vibe created by Eeva's spoken vocals, almost prophetic in tone, which has become a signature, recognizable style for the band. Just as Pessi Jouste's classical training is evident in the violin work, Aino Kallio's influence shines through on the piano; at times, the music evokes the atmosphere of chamber music, at others, Eastern and jazz styles reminiscent of Hiromi Uehara, or even the experimental approach of Alain Rochette (from the band Present). When the sound grows heavier, it becomes dense and dark, yet the strings and Eeva Rajakangas are always there, ensuring we never quite plunge over the precipice."Tarina" ventures into new territory; while Eeva sings and phrases with great freedom, she does so in tandem with a band that evokes the anarchic melodies of the Lounge Lizards, until the violins launch into a sort of tango reminiscent of the track "Palmiers En Pots" by the Belgian group Aksak Maboul. It is not even far-fetched to draw parallels with the Rock in Opposition scene; one can even detect traces of the early, defiant Bj�rk, alongside the bass-clarinet blues of Jaakko Arola."Vesi" evokes a violin-infused cabaret sung by Ute Lemper, yet the arrangements steer the sound toward danceable rhythms infused with punk currents, waves that surge in and recede. The band adapts perfectly to this variety of styles, skillfully navigating the challenge of maintaining overall cohesion. They stand as an impenetrable, unbreakable shield, much like the Baltic Shield, reflecting that Nordic light which lasts for months; a duration that pales in comparison to the enduring scope of their musical and artistic vision.

items._cn_summary: 芬兰九人乐团VIMMA首张专辑将北欧民谣根基与多元实验元素并置：以古典钢琴与小提琴为底色，Eeva Rajakangas的说话式演唱贯穿全作，时而朗诵时而吟唱，形成辨识度极高的声线签名。北欧传统音乐的肃穆与凯尔特旋律的明亮相交织，摇滚与放克律动后期介入，长笛段落令人联想到Jethro Tull。作品内部空间感处理讲究，留白与即兴段落塑造爵士氛围；多把提琴与萨克斯构建室内乐质感，同时注入不协和合唱、失真吉他与迷狂卡巴莱气质。乐团触及摇滚反对运动谱系，旋律线条带有Lounge Lizards式的无政府倾向与Aksak Maboul式的探戈变体。钢琴手Aino Kallio的学院派训练与Pessi Jouste的古典小提琴功底为整体提供骨架，使器乐在浓密沉重的段落中仍保持结构感而不至失控。

items.album: Tracks: October 5th, 2027
items.tags: industrial EBM goth dark electro post-punk
items.excerpt: The ID:UD Senior Staff will spare no expense and forsake no opportunity to check out shows related to Our Thing and report back to you, the concerned and engaged reader and listener. Alex headed out to Toronto for the weekend in order to finally see the oft-promised, never delivered (until now) miracle of a live Tear Garden set, while Bruce stayed closer to home and checked out the Vancouver instalment of the Immortalis tour, featuring Past Self, Pink Stiletto, ET, Ringinger, and Covert Forces.
items.body: The ID:UD Senior Staff will spare no expense and forsake no opportunity to check out shows related to Our Thing and report back to you, the concerned and engaged reader and listener. Alex headed out to Toronto for the weekend in order to finally see the oft-promised, never delivered (until now) miracle of a live Tear Garden set, while Bruce stayed closer to home and checked out the Vancouver instalment of the Immortalis tour, featuring Past Self, Pink Stiletto, ET, Ringinger, and Covert Forces. We’ll have a full discussion of both nights on this week’s podcast. Okay, admittedly these are shows we’d still be going to even if we didn’t run a website and podcast dedicated to this biz, but we might as well make a meal of it, no? On with this week’s tracks. The Sick Man Of Europe Statiqbloom, “A Grief Observed” Votive, the latest three-track release from now veteran electro-industrial cum dark techno project Statiqbloom does a nice job of triangulating most of the sounds Fade Kainer’s employed under that name over the past decade, from murky half-time power electronics on “Cut The Vine” to more straightforward distorted kicks on “Erased”. But despite its very brief run-time, it’s the sickly acidic programming of “A Grief Observed”, crawling beneath Kainer’s mutters which is reminding us of why we’ve loved his psychedelic approach to vintage post-industrial for so long. Votive by Statiqbloom The Sick Man of Europe, “Apathy” Some pleasingly minimal but still melodic synth action from the UK’s Sick Man of Europe sure is hitting the spot right now. Maybe it’s the insistent drum programming, or the beleeping bass and synthwork, or the punky feedback on the lead, but the contrast between those elements and the frustration and anger of the lyrics certainly gives this one some juice. The Intermittent Signal by The Sick Man Of Europe Nick Viola, “Soft Brutalism” Nick Viola’s name should ring a bell to regular readers, either for his excellent work as Fractured Transmission or his role in the defunct Death Camp Audio clique releases from about a decade back (or his role in US supergroup HexRx, going back further), but a new EP under his own name functions as a good reintroduction to the read on dark techno he’s been working on in recent years. Dense and icy washes of distortion keep the kicks from ever running riot and pushing the subtler cyber programming out of the frame. Soft Brutalism by Nick Viola ᚾᛟᚢ, “Break Like Frost” Nothing Nordvargr finds while digging into his archives is likely to be “pleasant” in any traditional sense of the word. But it’s interesting to hear something like this pulled from the vaults, the first (so far as we can determine) release under the “ᚾᛟᚢ” name, clarifying the nominative distinction between Nordvargr and Trepaneringsritualen’s Thomas Martin Ekelund in their collaborative ᚾᛟᚢ II // ᚦᛟᚦ ᚷᛁᚷ project. Regardless of name or origin the icy mood of this piece’s drifts of death industrial and dark ambient soundscapes are apparent from the moment it begins even without looking at its title, with some classic lo-fi cassette style recording. Trollkorset by ᚾᛟᚢ Then Comes Silence, “Remaker Redeemer” Sweden’s Then Comes Silence make the kind of muscly, synth-inflected goth rock that has never truly gone out of style in Europe. And to their credit, they do it well; where so many acts who attempt the style have neither the vocal charisma nor the hooks to pull it off, TCS has plenty of both to spare. “Remaker Redeemer” has all kinds of mood and atmosphere, but doesn’t skimp on a big jump up chorus, accented by some grindy basswork and syncopated drums that make it fit for the club or the headphones. Requiem Ballroom by THEN COMES SILENCE Ye Gods, “Outlier (single edit)” Oh, to live in a world where songs like Ye Gods’ “Outlier” could be actual radio play singles. Kidding aside, we’re obviously huge fans of Antoni Maiovvi’s work, especially in the sprawling and conceptual esoteric canvas that the producer has made of Ye Gods (hear our interview from last year here), and this cut is no exception. It’s rhythmic, weird, lovely and unnerving, and often both at the same time. New EP Los comes out mid-October, mark it on your halloween calendars. Los by Ye Gods The post Tracks: October 5th, 2027 appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items._cn_summary: 本期乐评聚焦多组暗潮与工业领域新作。Statiqbloom的《Votive》以三首短曲回顾其十年声响演变，从半速粗糙的电力电子到失真节奏，以及酸性合成器在低语人声下蠕动的迷幻感。The Sick Man of Europe的《Apathy》以极简旋律化的合成器与朋克反馈音色制造张力，歌词中的愤怒与配器形成鲜明对比。Nick Viola的《Soft Brutalism》展示近年暗潮技术探索，密集冰冷的失真织体包裹着细微的赛博节奏编程。ᚾᛟᚢ的《Break Like Frost》作为Nordvargr档案发掘之作，呈现其非传统美感，澄清了与Trepaneringsritualen主理人的名义区分。整体内容围绕地下工业与暗潮场景的现场与新作，兼具乐评与现场报道的双重价值。

items.body: “There are black silences, like thunderclouds, that burst into flashes of music,” H. G. Wells writes in Select Conversations with an Uncle. The phrase finds an almost literal visual counterpart in Jordan Reyes’s cover for Songs for Sad Poets Vol. III: a dense black expanse pressing against a bleached, nearly featureless sky, its uneven boundary resembling storm clouds seen in negative. It also anticipates a pivotal moment in “Sigils of Decay”, when the music comes to such an abrupt halt that, on first hearing, I had to check whether it was still playing. Out of that prolonged absence a low rumble eventually emerges, giving voice to the disquiet that runs through the latest collaboration between Siavash Amini & Eugene Thacker. The three pieces included are dedicated respectively to Vietnamese poet Hàn Mặc Tử, Brazilian Symbolist João da Cruz e Sousa and Austrian poet Nikolaus Lenau, figures connected by the tradition of the poète maudit. “Leprous Doubt”, for Hàn Mặc Tử, opens with dissonant textures, degraded sounds and sudden changes of register. It is unsettling and unsettled, meandering in unforeseen directions and making its discomfort palpable. The music pauses and resumes, pitching antagonistic forces against one another; moments of sweeping grandeur coexist with passages of intimate travail. It repeatedly attempts to steady itself before faltering again. Circular tones eventually lift to reveal the “glowing abyss” of Thacker’s poem, while intensifying drones recede until a solitary, quivering tone remains. “Sigils of Decay”, for Cruz e Sousa, pushes this instability into silence itself. The long interruption at its centre makes the eventual return of sound unusually physical. As the low frequencies slowly reassert themselves, muted fragments accumulate into a dark, suspended mass. Thacker writes of “muted music / woven by / night spiders”, an image that seems uncannily close to what Amini constructs: strands of sound gradually spun into a crepuscular firmament of drones and disarticulated fragments, only to loosen again. The connection with Cruz e Sousa is equally suggestive. His poetry transforms an inexplicable melancholy into a confrontation with the Infinite; Thacker condenses that metaphysical sadness into the colder “Dread of / Infinite space. / Dread of / Distant skies.” At nineteen minutes, “Dead Eyes, Dark Stars” is the album’s most expansive piece. Its opening is nocturnal, with celestial voices suspended above slumbering coils of sound. These gradually precipitate into increasingly abrasive textures, yet the music pulls itself back towards a softer harmonic balance. Timbral shifts become more pronounced as the underlying material turns metallic and resonant. Lenau’s recurring world of night, forests, barren landscapes, grief and death finds an oblique counterpart here: the landscape seems to have been emptied of narrative and retained as atmosphere, shadow and distant light. Voice assumes a much greater presence than on the first Songs for Sad Poets, although words never present themselves as intelligible text. Synthetic voices gather into spectral choirs and dissolve into the surrounding music, allowing Thacker’s poems to remain embedded within the pieces without requiring the listener to follow them line by line. The relationship between poetry and sound consequently operates through images, structures and emotional pressure: Hàn Mặc Tử’s diseased bodies and impossible skies, Cruz e Sousa’s metaphysical melancholy, Lenau’s nocturnal desolation. Each piece finally leaves a coda of silence. By then, Reyes’s cover feels increasingly inseparable from the music: darkness occupies most of the field, while its opposite persists beyond its ragged edge. H.G. Wells’s “black silences” provide an apt description of an album where silence continually threatens to swallow the music, yet also provides the space from which it can begin again. To lift the veil on the production process we have spoken directly to Saivash Amini. On the first Songs for Sad Poets, Eugene Thacker’s poems were never actually spoken; the words were translated into sound without becoming voice. On Vol. III, you take almost the opposite route, programming voice-synthesis software to perform the poems and then processing as many as forty voices until language becomes unintelligible. What interested you in bringing the human voice into the project only to erase its legibility again? Do you still think of these pieces as songs, or has the distinction between voice, text and sound become irrelevant? The idea of voice synthesis came out of a conversation with Eugene about his dislike of the human voice and the vocal music he actually liked like Ligeti’s requiem, where micropolyphony, among other techniques, were used to mask the intelligibility of the text and transform the human choir into something entirely different. I have much of the liberty of a large choir in my DAW with voice synthesis software. It’s not actually a human voice, so I can make a sound very modulated and affected when singing. And I can have as many as I want to have, as long as my CPU can handle it, so micropolyphony can be much more extreme and differently intricate. And yes, I do think of these as songs, they are structured around the poem. Just not conventional songs with known musical structures. But that’s when I’m making them. There’s no point trying to find the points of reference to poems if you’re just listening, they are trying to convey the same thing. Listening closely to the three pieces, decay seems to function as a compositional process rather than simply as an atmosphere. “Leprous Doubt” repeatedly loses substance and regains it; “Sigils of Decay” moves through accumulation and withdrawal; and the nineteen-minute “Dead Eyes, Dark Stars” forms large masses of sound that gradually weather away, return and finally disappear. This concern with appearance, erosion and reconstitution also seems connected to Eidolon, Caligo and Severed Like the Red Moon, where sounds are made to float, bleed, collapse, be mutilated and reassembled. Has this become a central way for you to think about musical form? Yes and no, I have been more and more putting focus in making structures and out evolving and directional textures made out of different approaches to generating harmony. It’s not all I think about when making pieces but more likely the result of intentional putting together of smaller directional elements of different duration. So the micro is what determines the macro, and a lot of the times I’m thinking of micro. The poets invoked on Vol. III come from very different linguistic and cultural histories: Hàn Mặc Tử and Vietnam’s “Chaos” school, João da Cruz e Sousa and Brazilian Symbolism, and Nikolaus Lenau and the tradition of Weltschmerz. How did you and Eugene Thacker arrive at these particular figures, and what drew you to bringing such different poetic traditions together within the same musical cycle? That’s all Eugene’s side of the project but the thread that links them all is in the Poet Maudit term which the title comes from. They all fit that category. Much of your recent work has begun from literary or historical material: Ibn Sina on eremos, Xavier Villaurrutia on The Sweat of Earth, early Iranian piano recordings and Malakoot on Caligo, as well as Houshang Golshiri on Severed Like the Red Moon. In each case, the source seems to act less as something to illustrate than as a force that changes the way you treat sound. What does literature give you that a purely musical starting point does not, and has worked so closely with Eugene Thacker altered the way you now read a text as a composer? Using literature for my work goes to my first album. Then I have three collaborations with Matt Finney which were based on his reading his poems and sending them to me. Serus had a strong relationship with the writings of Blanchot I can go on… I find using literature gives me a structure and image which I can turn into sound worlds. I can imagine something to convey that image. I find that very exciting but a lot of background work before the project starts is done on purely musical material. Working with Eugene changed my workflow in general and made my relationship with literature deeper than it was before, and it gave me a lot to think about when it comes to making sound that conveys what one word is telling me. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._genre: dark ambient / drone / contemporary classical / experimental
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由伊朗裔音乐家Siavash Amini与哲学家Eugene Thacker合作完成，献给三位poète maudit诗人：越南的Hàn Mặc Tử、巴西的Cruz e Sousa和奥地利的Lenau。三首作品以不和谐织体、降质声音与突然的力度断裂构建不安的情绪氛围，经常在试图稳定时再度失稳，沉默本身成为作品的重要组成部分——中段长时间的中断使声音的回归具有罕见的物理性。低频嗡鸣缓慢重现，暗色悬置的质量逐渐累积，编织成黄昏般的声场。十九分钟的终曲以夜空般的天体声音开场，逐渐沉淀为磨蚀性织体，音色变化趋向金属化与共振感，叙事被抽离，仅余氛围、阴影与远光。

items.album: Anushka Chkheidze + Robert Lippok :: The Sky Was Out of Tune (Morr Music)
items.excerpt: Natural recordings, soft rhythms, distortion, metallic noises, melody, and digital artifacts continually lean against one another without settling. By the end it feels less like eight compositions and more like half an hour spent inside a system that was continuously adjusting itself while you were listening, and never quite finished. Everything feels connected by residue The Sky Was Out of Tune by Anushka Chkheidze + Robert Lippok   Anushka Chkheidze and Robert Lippok make sense together.
items.body: Natural recordings, soft rhythms, distortion, metallic noises, melody, and digital artifacts continually lean against one another without settling. By the end it feels less like eight compositions and more like half an hour spent inside a system that was continuously adjusting itself while you were listening, and never quite finished. Everything feels connected by residue The Sky Was Out of Tune by Anushka Chkheidze + Robert Lippok   Anushka Chkheidze and Robert Lippok make sense together. Chkheidze is a Georgian composer and producer based in the Netherlands. Lippok is Berlin, To Rococo Rot, Raster Noton, installation work, decades of treating electronic sound as material that gets layered, cut, reshaped, and left partially unresolved. They met in Tbilisi in 2019 through a workshop program, worked together on Glacier Music II, then built that into Uncontrollable Thoughts, their first joint album for Morr Music in 2025. Morr Music has spent decades in that specific space between electronica, ambient, post-rock, and minimal composition—múm, The Notwist, B. Fleischmann, music where texture and atmosphere carry as much weight as conventional structure. A natural home for this collaboration. The Sky Was Out of Tune pushes further. Eight pieces, titled only with Roman numerals, and they really don’t function as separate tracks so much as sections of one continuous object. That makes sense, the music grew out of a live performance at Berlin’s Neue Nationalgalerie. Everything feels connected by residue. A texture disappears and something remains behind it. A rhythmic idea dissolves into ambience. A metallic sound becomes the thing guiding the next section without announcing itself as such. “I” opens with what sounds like field recording, natural ambience, small bell-like tones, rattling, paper movement, objects handled close to a microphone. Hard to identify exactly what some of those sounds are. Records that begin this way can immediately position themselves as documentary field recording works where the environment becomes the subject. Here the material behaves differently. It’s preparation. Those sounds establish a physical space before synthetic material gets pushed into it. Tiny rhythmic impulses sit beneath the surface :: That becomes one of the strongest ideas running through the record. Chkheidze and Lippok are extremely good at preparing the listener for something before revealing what it is. Ambience gathers density. Distortion arrives gradually. Tiny rhythmic impulses sit beneath the surface before becoming clearer. Metallic sounds enter and disappear like objects moving through the stereo field. No obvious drops. No resolutions. They build toward changes in texture instead, which is a harder thing to make feel earned. Their process on Uncontrollable Thoughts involved long improvisations, selecting ideas afterward, sending projects between one another. Chkheidze contributing drums, piano, vocals. Lippok adding noise, harmony, sometimes reshaping the entire piece. He’s described his production as primarily layering, constructing, collaging, not sitting at a keyboard writing chord progressions. You can hear that philosophy all over this record. Compared to Uncontrollable Thoughts, The Sky Was Out of Tune is more dissolved. The previous album still had recognizable individual pieces—”Bird Song,” “Rainbow Road,” soft beats, organ drones, clear rhythmic personalities moving between tracks. Boundaries here have almost completely disappeared. Uncontrollable Thoughts felt like two musicians improvising compositions. This feels like those same two musicians improvising an environment. The rhythm is still present but behaves more like weather than percussion. Digital texture and ambience overlapping :: Soft electro rhythms surface throughout, especially when the album settles into its more defined sections. Nothing becomes overly forceful. Even when distortion enters it feels incorporated into the ambience rather than placed over it. There are moments that recall the softer edges of early Mille Plateaux material, digital texture and ambience overlapping until it becomes difficult to decide which one you’re actually listening to. The late 90s and early 2000s electronica sensibility is present throughout, that specific understanding that small rhythmic gestures can carry enormous emotional weight if given room. “VII” is the most interesting section on the record and it lasts 35 seconds. The glitches become more exposed, textures start colliding, and suddenly the album sounds like it might move somewhere completely different—like a corrupted transitional file that accidentally became part of the release. Its short duration is what gives it impact. “VII” functions as a doorway into “VIII” rather than a standalone piece. An introduction to the outro. And that tiny moment reveals something about the whole record, Chkheidze and Lippok are comfortable letting an idea exist only as long as it needs to. A texture doesn’t have to develop into a full track. A rhythmic pattern can appear for seconds and disappear. Something can sound important and still never return. The title describes the music unusually well. A sky being out of tune doesn’t mean the environment has collapsed, it means something familiar has shifted slightly enough that you start paying closer attention. That’s what happens here. Natural recordings, soft rhythms, distortion, metallic noises, melody, and digital artifacts continually lean against one another without settling. By the end it feels less like eight compositions and more like half an hour spent inside a system that was continuously adjusting itself while you were listening, and never quite finished. The Sky Was Out of Tune is available on Morr Music. items._cn_summary: Anushka Chkheidze与Robert Lippok合作的专辑《The Sky Was Out of Tune》收录八首以罗马数字命名的作品，整体更像一个连续运行的系统而非独立曲目集合。专辑源于柏林Neue Nationalgalerie的现场演出，自然录音、田野采样、微小节奏脉冲、扭曲失真、金属质感的噪音与数字残响层层叠加，彼此渗透却不形成明确的解决。自然环境声作为铺垫引入合成素材，氛围逐渐积聚密度，节奏隐现于表面之下，金属声响在立体声场中穿行而无明确的高潮点。两人通过长期即兴创作与异地文件交换完成制作，将鼓、钢琴、人声与电子处理交织，使专辑在电子、氛围、田野录音与后摇滚之间持续调整自身状态，始终保持未完成的不安定感。

items.body: A mesmerizing collision of ambient, jazz, electronics and ritualistic textures, this album unfolds like a deep-space journey that never loses its human pulse. Trumpet drifts through electronic vastness Fade In Brighter Age by Pulsar + Demetrio Cecchitelli   Mahorka has a busy schedule and quite an enormous back catalog, covering various electronic music, from ambient to dub, noise and radically experimental. Confirmed sound artists meet new promising ones in the course of indie, challenging music with no regard for major commercial tendencies. I’ve never heard of Pulsar (Leonardo Pucci) before, but I must say he perfectly teams up with Demitrio Cecchitelli. I’m more familiar with the work of Cecchitelli, notably with the sumptuous Empetus (published years ago by Midira). The addition of trumpet player Jacopo Buda to the soundscapes gives an enriched musical meaning to the album, playing the card of instrumental ambient music with partly experimental-jazzy tones and expansive improvs which evolve on dynamic electronic textures. What we can listen to here is nothing less than a furiously enthralling and original musical trip which starts masterfully with the ethno-ritual and spaced-out “Cosmic Dream”. Such a gorgeous piece with its perpetual circular rhythms covered by inspiring and gently minimal trumpet melodic shifts. It is meticulously crafted without being purely ambient, as it conjugates a vast array of influences, from Buddhist-Zen musical attributes to early minimalism and atmospheric, then bassy, chilled-out vibes. It suggests immensity and nature-like vastness, with its colorful timbres resonating in divine harmony. It is a sprawling track with a magnificent development, always suspenseful, melodically ethereal and dynamic. The second track (“Expanding Light”) also operates a nice syncretism and musical dialogue between acoustic ingredients, wind instruments and electronics, but here we enter a more downtempo, softly moving ambience, less lyrical and tripped-out but equally good and perfectly elaborated. The title track (“Fade in Brighter Age”) almost provides a softly moving dream-pop quality, built on guitars, vibrant chords and slowly enveloping wind sequences, largely embracing a lonesome path and a feeling of consciousness at night. All in all, a varied and semi-jazzy atmospheric ambient album with a flowing cinematic edge. Absolutely recommended and easily one of my personal favorites of this year. For fans of John Hassell, Harold Budd, Peter Knight, Loscil, Bersanin Quartett, Nala Sinephro, and Floating Points. Fade In Brighter Age is available on Mahorka. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以小号为核心乐器，与电子音效和仪式化律动交织，构建出兼具环境氛围与即兴张力的声音空间。Pulsar与Demetrio Cecchitelli的合作呈现出多层次的声音设计：循环节奏铺底，小号旋律线在其上方自由漂浮，形成开放式的对话结构。作品融合了佛教禅意、早期简约主义元素与电子合成器纹理，配器涵盖管乐、原声器乐与电声音响，呈现出电影感与冥想感的双重特质。专辑从节奏感较强的开场曲逐渐过渡到更内省的氛围段落，音乐语汇在动态与静态之间持续转换。发行厂牌Mahorka专注于独立实验音乐领域，与专辑的艺术取向一致。整体制作注重音色空间与情绪流动，作品之间既有连续性又各具色彩，是将即兴爵士逻辑融入环境电子框架的一次成熟实践。

items.body: Jesu Aparicio is a Spanish artist who sees himself first and foremost as a DJ, and only secondly as a producer. He has been active in the Spanish club scene for years and won me over this year with his album “Human Control”. The album was released on Jesu’s own label, Espacio Cielo, in collaboration with Mots Music. The name Parissior may not ring a bell for many, but I highly recommend this work to anyone with an interest in Dark-Techno and EBM. The album’s title and theme reflect the increasingly complex relationship between humans, technology, control, and the systems that shape our daily lives. By combining dark electronic sounds with an atmosphere that is both unsettling and intriguing, Parissior creates music that invites the listener to look beyond the surface. The album evokes the atmosphere and danceability of the 1990s Frankfurt Techno scene while adding a distinctly contemporary twist. For me, this record is one of this year’s best discoveries, making it the perfect time to meet the artist behind Parissior and talk to him about “Human Control”, his influences, and his approach to music. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Parissior interview Q: Could you give us some background on your musical activities, which apparently began quite some time ago as a DJ and eventually evolved into producing, leading to the Parissior project? Jesu: I began DJing professionally in my native Cantabria in 2001, playing Techno and House under my own name, ‘Jesu Aparicio’. In 2004, I moved to Salamanca, where I became a resident DJ at several venues, including Cubic Club, Submarino and Beatz. Those years were a major learning experience for me and gave me a much deeper understanding of the music industry. I eventually opened my own venue, Clavel Ocho, which featured an upstairs floor dedicated to Electronic music called Espacio Cielo – the name I would later revive for my record label. I started producing around 2004 and, over the years, explored many different styles and released music under several aliases. Altogether, I have released more than 600 tracks. I have always considered myself a DJ first and a producer second, although these days I actually spend more time producing music than performing as a DJ. Around 2011, I began to feel restricted by playing the same styles, so I created the Parissior alias as a way to broaden my musical horizons. It allowed me to explore funkier and more cosmic sounds, as well as Electro and Italo-Disco, eventually moving towards the EBM-influenced sound that has become an important part of the project’s identity. Q: Personally, I find it interesting that you moved into music production after starting out as a DJ – a role that naturally exposes you to a vast amount of music. This perhaps also helps explain the eclectic nature of your own work. What did your experience as a DJ bring to your approach to music-making, and what were some of your key influences and muses? Jesu: As a DJ, I have always been very eclectic and curious, and I have always enjoyed collecting music from a wide range of genres: ’80s music, Funk and Soul, Disco, Electro, House, Techno, Big Beat, Breaks… Salamanca had many clubs and bars, each with a very distinct musical identity, so playing there pushed you to dig deeper, discover new sounds and adapt to very different audiences. Being exposed to such a vast amount of music has undoubtedly had a major influence on the way I produce. You learn to recognize the formulas and ideas that make each genre work, and then reinterpret and adapt them to your own musical language. My influences have naturally evolved over the years, but I could never leave out Joy Division and New Order, Talking Heads, The Prodigy, The Chemical Brothers, Pet Shop Boys, Andrew Weatherall, Primal Scream or LCD Soundsystem, among many others. Q: You released the album “Human Control” this year, which, as I understand it, was not originally conceived as an album. How did it all come about, and how did the concept of “Human Control” take shape? Or did the concept emerge only afterwards, almost imposing itself on the music? Jesu: As you rightly say, the album was not initially planned as such. I had three tracks that I had deliberately held back from releasing on any label because they felt more personal, less focused on the dancefloor, and did not really fit with any of the EPs I had previously released. Almost without realizing it, I had incorporated phrases and messages into those tracks that shared a certain underlying theme: a defense of the analogue world and a critique of the artificiality and falsehood that often surround today’s digital culture and social media. Once I recognized that common thread, I decided to compose a series of new tracks around those original three and gradually shape the whole thing into an album. The first track I created with that intention was “Human Control.” It features a sample from a speech by Greta Thunberg at the UN Climate Action Summit, in which she delivers a passionate and somewhat dramatic rebuke to the world’s leaders. That track ultimately gave both the album and its central concept a clear identity. Q: What can you tell us about the writing and production process behind the album? What did you focus on most, and what were the different stages you went through to bring “Human Control” to completion? What tools and equipment did you work with, and what were the biggest challenges along the way? Jesu: One of the album’s defining features – and also its biggest challenge – was the decision to deliberately limit the amount of hardware and software I used on each track. I find that working within those kinds of restrictions forces me to be more creative, especially compared with having thousands of possibilities available in the form of plug-ins. My process was generally to choose a small palette of sound sources for each track, record the main parts, and then reshape and develop them through processing. For example, every synthesizer part on “True Connection” came from the Waldorf Pulse 2. Most of the basslines on the album were created with an analogue clone of the Roland SH-101, which I also used to design many of the drum sounds, while the Acid lines came from the Behringer TD-3. Another synthesizer that played a major role throughout the album was the Model D, and I also incorporated parts I had recorded years earlier with my Roland JX-3P. On the software side, I used Ableton’s stock plug-ins alongside Massive and Omnisphere. Massive was the only synthesizer used on “Human Control,” while Omnisphere appears more sparingly on some of the other tracks, mainly providing polyphonic textures. I also enjoy running synthesizers through effects pedals to create new tones and textures, while the vocals were processed using the Roland VT-4 and a variety of VST effects. Ultimately, the main focus was to get as much character and variety as possible from a relatively small and carefully chosen set of tools. Q: With this album, you explore themes such as digital identity, technology, artificial validation, and the relationship between humans and machines. Could you tell us a little more about these themes, and to what extent did they influence your decision to release the album on vinyl? To me, the physical format almost feels like a response to – or a reaction against – the increasingly digital nature of our lives. And if so, why vinyl rather than cassette? Jesu: That was exactly the idea. Releasing the album on vinyl was, in many ways, a reaction against the digitalisation of almost every aspect of our lives. Particularly since the pandemic, it often feels as though people’s lives have been reduced to the online alter egos they create on platforms such as Instagram – showing the world only what they want others to see and projecting lifestyles that they are not necessarily living in reality. Releasing a record on vinyl had also been unfinished business for me with Espacio Cielo, so my own album felt like the perfect opportunity to take that step. There was an economic reason as well: digital sales are falling every year as listening increasingly shifts towards streaming platforms such as Spotify, yet the royalties these services pay are extremely unfair. Sometimes you barely earn enough to buy a hamburger, which makes it very difficult for an independent label to remain financially sustainable. I also feel that digital music is more ephemeral. It disappears more quickly, becomes outdated faster and struggles to hold people’s attention. A vinyl record has a physical presence and a sense of permanence: people tend to spend more time with it, and it can remain part of their lives for years. In that sense, the format became a natural extension of the album’s concept. To be honest, I never seriously considered releasing it on cassette. It is a very nostalgic format, but I also think that very few people still own the equipment needed to play tapes. Of course, the same issue exists to some extent with vinyl, but many DJs have kept their Technics turntables, and the fact that the company has released new models such as the MK7 gives me some reason for optimism. Vinyl also has a much stronger connection to my own history as a DJ and to the culture surrounding this music. From now on, we plan to slow down the label’s digital release schedule and gradually release more records on vinyl. Who knows – perhaps in a few years we will release exclusively on vinyl. It is something I am seriously considering. Q: Where do you draw the line today between human control and the control we voluntarily surrender to technology? In what sense do you see the title and concept of “Human Control” as a warning, an observation, or perhaps even a personal confession? How do you see humans evolving alongside technological progress, and what role do you think the musician will play in that relationship? Jesu: That boundary is becoming increasingly blurred. There is no denying that we will benefit enormously from technological progress and that it will make many aspects of our lives easier. However, when it comes to art and culture, I believe we need to preserve certain principles and ensure that convenience and automation do not replace human intention, creativity and genuine expression. In that sense, “Human Control” is both an observation and a warning. Technology itself is not the enemy; the real question is how much control and creative autonomy we are willing to surrender to it. We should remain the ones making the decisions, with technology serving as a tool rather than dictating the creative process. At the same time, I think a counter-movement is beginning to emerge – one that will bring back a greater appreciation for craftsmanship, physical formats and live music. I am already seeing clubs programming exclusively live sets, as well as all-vinyl nights, which I find very encouraging. Perhaps the musician’s role in this new relationship will be precisely to preserve that human element: spontaneity, imperfection and a genuine connection with the audience. Q: Do you also perform your Parissior tracks live, or do they mainly form part of your DJ sets? How does that work in practice, and what can we expect from Parissior in the near future? Jesu: I have always considered myself more of a DJ than a producer, even though, since the pandemic, I have actually spent more time producing than performing. I love playing DJ sets, and while I already have enough of my own material prepared to develop a full live show, the right opportunity has not yet presented itself. For the moment, Parissior’s music therefore appears mainly within my DJ sets. I have performed hybrid sets using hardware, but fees are sometimes so limited today that paying for additional luggage to transport equipment becomes impractical. The same applies to vinyl: I play vinyl locally, but when I travel, I usually perform with CDJs for exactly the same reason. Because of my day job, I only play around five or six gigs a year, and promoters generally approach me to perform DJ sets. However, I would definitely like to explore the live format when the right opportunity and conditions come along. About Parissior Parissior is the alias of Spanish DJ and producer Jesu Aparicio. He began DJing professionally in his native Cantabria in 2001 under his own name, playing Techno and House. In 2004 he moved to Salamanca, where he became a resident DJ at venues including Cubic Club, Submarino and Beatz, and later opened his own venue, Clavel Ocho, whose upstairs floor, Espacio Cielo, was dedicated to electronic music. He started producing around 2004 and has released more than 600 tracks under various aliases. He created the Parissior alias in 2011 to explore Electro, Italo-Disco and EBM-influenced sounds beyond his earlier productions. Parissior has released singles and EPs since at least 2016, including “Could I Drown In Your Desire” and “Dance To The Groove” (Spa In Disco), followed by “Let Them Dance” (Hot Digits Music, 2017) and further EPs and compilation appearances for Golden Soul Records. From “Back To Earth” (2020) onward he has worked mainly through Espacio Cielo, the label he revived from his former venue’s name, releasing further singles, EPs and compilation tracks including “Battle Cry” (2021), “Raver In The Booth” and “Full of Stars” (2023), and the Skylax release “Antennae” (2024). “Human Control”, Parissior’s first full-length album, was released on Espacio Cielo in collaboration with Mots Music. Side-Line reviewed the album in September 2026, describing it as a mix of Dark-Techno and EBM. This interview follows that review.
