items.body: To celebrate and commemorate John Coltrane’s 100 th birthday, drummer extraordinaire Don Berman will reprise at the Chapel Performance Space in Seattle his original composition, 'Ascension Northwest', written in the spirit of Coltrane’s Ascension (Impulse!, 1966). As in the original, Berman has11 musicians playing a series of mantras interspersed with spirited soloing over improvised support from subsets of other players, including a double-bass duet. A preview of this year’s performance written by Paul Rauch appears in Seattle’s Earshot Jazz magazine: https://online.fliphtml5.com/risyt/Earshot_Jazz_09_2026/#p=13 You can hear earlier versions of 'Ascension Northwest' released here: https://threshold24.bandcamp.com/album/ascension‑northwest As a contribution for the FJB Coltrane birthday column, I’ve asked the 11 musicians performing 'Ascension Northwest' (myself included) to reflect on Coltrane’s Ascension and its impact on their musical journey. Below, our answers (gingerly edited). The questionnaire is reproduced at the very end. Tom Varner (French horn) 1. I knew about Coltrane and loved his music from his time with Miles, and also his ‘classic’ quartet recordings, when I was in high school and getting into jazz. I did not know about Ascension until a bit later, perhaps early in college. Even though I loved Ornette Coleman, and even Albert Ayler, I must say that very late Coltrane and Ascension was a bit :”Whoa! This is too heavy for me!” at first listen. I think I wanted to hear the ‘melodic line’ no matter how ‘out’ it was, and this music went beyond that. Eventually I grew to love it, letting go of the ‘I must hear a clear line’ worry and just enjoying being carried away in the power of the SOUND. I.e., that sound of a ‘scary but then NOT scary’ glorious totality of several improvisers all going full steam ahead at once. The JCOA Michael Mantler ‘Communications’ 3-LP set, from 1968, with Pharoah Sanders and other greats, was a kind of bridge for me to the world of Ascension . To a kind of ‘beautiful crying battle’ as opposed to just noise. Within one or two years, I was open to playing in those settings! 1a. Ascension opened up a new world of “multiple new sound-creating improvisers” creating new avenues that were not ‘just’ chord change or single-line orientated. From then on, Coltrane’s world and the worlds of, say, Xenakis and Ligeti, were not so far apart! 1b.Moving into the ‘90s, I worked with ensembles that had 6, 7, 8 winds with bass and drums. I was going for that high energy sound where it was ‘ok’ to not hear individual single lines and just get swept away in the sound. The best example of this is my own “Death at the Right Time,” on “The Mystery of Compassion” on Soul Note (1992). 5 saxes, three low brass, bass and drums. 1c. Ascension kind of gave us ‘permission’ to create beautiful and powerful structures with very little or no written music, just ideas, and trusting that the improvisers will create a lasting artwork on the spot. I love that! 2. This is very corny, but at age 18, I clearly remember thinking “Well, remember, Tom, if things get bad in the future, or very challenging, don’t forget to listen to Coltrane—that music is healing. That music will always be there.” And, I would also simply say, “thank you, Mr. Coltrane.” Jim Knodle (trumpet) I heard Ascension when it was released in 1966. I regard it as a companion to Ornette's double quartet project Free Jazz . The interaction between Scott LaFaro and Jimmy Garrison is really something! Perry Robinson told me that the whole thing started at the Federal Prison in Lexington where everyone practiced in the same room at the same time. They didn’t want them to rehearse, so they just played ad hoc . Kenny Mandell (alto sax) 1. I was probably 19 when I first heard Ascension . 1972 or so. Being in college, I had heard free jazz players in NYC, and I knew Sun Ra’s music. Ascension was way more organized than a lot of Sun Ra’s music insofar as it kept the traditional jazz form where there was thematic material followed by solos. There are motifs but there aren’t any chord changes to speak of, and there is some degree of cacophony. Depending on the player, some of the solos were more traditional, others were, I would say, divinely inspired, like Eric Dolphy’s. In my listening life at that time, I quickly went from Led Zeppelin to the Art Ensemble, Albert Ayler, Archie Shepp, and Cecil Taylor. Most people thought I was crazy. I related to the energy of it. The dissonance never bothered me per se. Ascension showed me that the big band format could be stretched. The rock stuff was relatively static in comparison. Hendrix was close. Everybody else stayed in the form. I see Ascension as important but not seminal. It’s certainly part of the canon. 1b. I’ve put many large groups together over the years. Part of the game plan for large group improvisation is to establish a level of trust. I’ve learned to pick people who are comfortable recognizing that the traditional limits or strictures put on playing are actually optional, and one can use or not use those depending on what sort of statement the whole piece wants to make. Murray Bookchin’s Post-Scarcity Anarchism (1971, 1986) was pivotal (early 1970s) for me as much as any of this music. I tried to use those principles in music and in organizing. My book some day will be called The Tyranny of Harmony . Piano chords in particular limit your choices as an improvisor. It’s also the case that as I’ve gotten older and found that the audience just hasn’t been there for totally unstructured, large-form music, I’ve tended to select pieces or write pieces that give the audience some sort of repeated motif to ground their listening experience. 1c. Ascension opened the door. After A Love Supreme (1965), people thought Coltrane took an extreme left turn into the world of sound exploration as it could be manifested in improvisation and group interaction. Ascension put into stark reality the challenges of making and of listening to that kind of music. I don’t think they got to the level that the Art Ensemble of Chicago did over the years, and some of Cecil’s groups that stayed together for years: Jimmy Lyons, Sirone, Andrew Cyrille, they practiced incessantly and got telepathic. 2. John Coltrane had an obsession with achieving a certain sound. Coltrane—his essence for me–is that ceaseless searching. This is what I love about music probably the most, it’s that it never ends. Dick Valentine (tenor sax) I reflected at length on the questions you posed, and on the evolution of my attitudes, responses and relations with Coltrane’s music, which I understand in a context of almost 60 years trying to educate myself and participate in contemporary expressions of Great Black Music. In the end, despite that his recorded output made a tremendous impact on my playing ‑‑ and was a singular factor in motivating my drive to make music ‑‑ I think it fair to say Ascension , the recording, has not occupied as big a space in my development or conceptualization as some other works. I played in Don Berman's three presentations of Ascension Northwest in 2016, and I'm very pleased indeed to get to do it again on the Coltrane centenary. I really cherish the privilege of participating with artists the caliber of those whom Don has persuaded. I look around the room at the assemblage of musical knowledge, emotional depth, technical proficiency, and aesthetic ambition, I am inspired and amazed and humbled. I’m long past accepting that I will never "understand" society. It seems to me the “order that governs power and human relations” in our real world is founded on out‑of‑date assumptions regarding what humanity needs to flourish. I know that there are many people aware of this damaging misalignment, and I can tell they mostly share my frustration that fixing large‑scale misalignments is not in the offing, thanks precisely to the systems that govern the distribution of power and dictate humans' relationship with real resources. So, on John Coltrane's centenary, we'll gather musicians, players and audience in celebration. In a sense, a roomful is perhaps a model of “society.” Everyone in the room will have some mental image of what constitutes a successful event ‑‑ in context, the definition of the community “flourishing,” right? As players, we have the responsibility to provide physical, audible inputs to the outcome. There is a bit of magic to what may happen here. Each player contributes to the global fabric, whose nature he may not predict. It’s understood that coordinated inputs are in some sense a prerequisite for success, and communication is required for coordination. How is communication achieved? By the act that constitutes that player’s input. It’s a bit recursive, to say the least! Neil Welch (tenor sax) 1. Ascension came my way when I was 15 or 16. I picked up the album in cd format at a record store. This was my first experience with Trane’s music on Impulse!. I picked up the album out of curiosity. I was initially struck by three things: 1. The album cover ‑‑ Coltrane the seeker, looking beyond himself, and beyond us to something cosmic. 2. The length of the album: Until this point, I didn't know that a ‘jazz’ album could be +/‑ 40 minutes in length. 3. The cd version had takes 1 and 2, which made it a double album. It was the most expensive CD I had ever bought. The response for me was immediate. I felt the album opened with a declarative question. Coltrane begins with a theme, but it is incomplete. The tonic is ‘missing’ from the first note he plays. He asks the band a question with only the partial theme, and leaves it to the band to complete that theme. Ascension felt to me a major and inevitable document in Coltrane’s music from this period. The emotional intensity of his solos, and what he was asking of a small group, had reached a tipping point. I found it deeply humbling and revealing that he used the vehicle of a communal sound to further amplify the concept of the jazz musician as soloist and group collaborator. 1a. After Ascension , I understood that in musical conversation, a powerful theme could be stated with brevity. A short theme can grant space for a complex response of virtually any length. 1b. Ascension helped me to experience song length as a durational mind-set. A song could, and ought to be, exactly the length needed to fulfill its musical and emotional aims. 1c .Ascension is, for me, an album of colliding forces and the unity of embracing those forces towards a common mission. It’s like people in a building. All these souls one floor atop the other. Different lives, worldviews, needs, hurts, wants, but all share the same vertical massing. If that building is on fire, they are invested in each other's outcome. They’ve looked in the eyes of those people in the elevator. 2. Can we as a society still sit with, and grapple with in real time, discordance in art‑making? Can intensity of sound and emotion hold space for us in our lives and aid us in the journey of deeper personal growth? Steve Meyer (alto sax) 1. I must have been 14 or 15. I was just getting into Coltrane and came across Ascension at my local record store. At that point I’d only known some of his earlier quartet work and work with Miles. Seeing that this was a larger group piqued my interest. And I recognized the names of a lot of heavy players, though I doubt I’d heard most of them at that point, so thought it would be a good album. After getting back home, I’m in my bedroom and put on the album. I don’t know what I was expecting but not too far into the first side (the first ensemble part) I knew it wasn’t for me. I didn’t know what to make of it, and it didn’t speak to me. I think I finished the first side but didn’t listen to the second. A few years went by before I was ready to give it another try. I was still an adventurous listener, so my first reaction didn’t turn me off from listening to other “out”/free musics which I grew to appreciate and enjoy more and more. 1a. If I don’t like what I hear on first listen, I remind myself that there are works of art out there that I’m not ready for. Music will speak to us when we’re ready to hear it. 1b. While I was listening to more out music in my teens it was years later before I played free music – at least with others. In high school this wasn’t the kind of music most of my musician friends would be into. Even with the one or two who weren’t opposed to it, we never thought to attempt it ourselves, at least not in any serious way, sticking to more standard jazz and the fusion music of the day. (This is early 80s, btw.) Even later, people I played with tended to be more conventional in the foundation of their music. These days I’m fortunate to have a community of musicians who embrace free/creative music. And, I have more confidence in myself to nudge the conversation that way when playing with others that I think will be receptive to it. 1c. I tend to not view music through a sociological lens, but Ascension and similar music has made me consider the normative orders of music in the US. Mainly, they’ve shown me there are a lot of stories to be told and a lot of different ways to tell them. 2. I want to thank Coltrane for his music and inspiration. The question to ask myself: how can I harness the focus and questing spirit of Trane? Eric Ring (piano) While A Love Supreme was life changing at 18, I’d surprisingly never heard Ascension prior to preparing for this performance. Don Berman (composer, drums ) 1. A sax player at my summer Maine resort job, a student of Jackie McLean, had introduced me to Coltrane’s Live at Birdland (Impulse!, 1964). This was 1972. I heard an amazing spiritual element in John Coltrane's music when I heard his quartet play “Alabama.” It struck me incredibly deeply and I have adored jazz and playing jazz ever since. (The piece was a deeply moving eulogy to the victims of bombing of the 16th street Baptist church in Birmingham, Alabama.) A couple of years later, in my junior year of college, I heard Ascension and realized that Trane had helped jazz expand its scope enormously to express a wider range of feelings. With the Ascension session, jazz composition and form had evolved light years from the beginnings of jazz decades earlier. After Ascension , there was now a huge universe of possibilities for jazz musicians to explore in their work. 1a.As I got further into jazz I particularly loved Miles Davis and John Coltrane, because I saw how each had evolved continuously throughout their musical journeys, from one period and chapter and style to another. The way I think about music and music making after Ascension is part and parcel of how I feel about music and art in general. All of the art forms have a rich and magical history. If you have studied and played music for years and years, you have to discover who you are and what your aesthetic is. 1b. For me, Ascension is part of what guided me further into freer playing and improvising in the last 20 years. Creating my own compositions has become more important for me. I organize pieces that contain both written and improvised sections. For this I select musicians that can both interpret written compositions and also improvise very well. 2. I would ask others: How does Coltrane’s music move you and make you feel about what feelings or sounds you play and express when you play? The world is full of a truly amazing variety of music. There are masters playing in each of those styles. I would ask others who take music seriously to open their minds and make sure they hear the music of master creators, live when possible, and in as many styles as possible. Master the basic fundamentals, and take music as seriously as Trane did. For those just seeking fun, that is fine too. A lot of striving people in the arts take things too seriously, especially when they become too self-absorbed and their egos interfere with what they are attempting to do as musicians. As the great pianist and educator Kenny Werner teaches his students and readers, “your value as a human being is not based upon how well you play a musical instrument.” Gregg Miller (baritone sax) 1. Around 1997 I bought a used CD copy of the compilation, The Major Works of John Coltrane (GRP Records, 1992) which included both takes of Ascension as well as Om , Kulu Se Mama , and Selflessness . I was stunned at the difference in intent between those recordings and Giant Steps . In Giant Steps , I heard a restless cramming of as many notes as quickly as possible within structures that could barely contain them. In Ascension , Coltrane had left that set of problems behind in favor of a compositional form that foregrounded the free-playing (and listening, or not listening) of every other player, a dense maelstrom that produced its own power without regard to or in opposition to or transcending of the traditional tropes of organized sound. To my ears, there was still an evident structuredness to the resultant noise, but full-on interplay was now the method and the lesson. It felt to me like a releasing of mutual respect, a lifting of repression inherent in most musics, and a deliberate shifting of power dynamics from a singular ordered mind that commands obedience (and players willingly, often reverently submitting to that control) to the shared embrace of others who jointly participate. Messy, but beautiful. I was studying a lot of Habermas at the time, and so for me, the link between music-making and communicative action was an easy one to see/hear and understand. I wasn’t playing free music (or any music) at the time, but the seed had been sown without me knowing it. 1a. In the late 1990s I would listen to Ascension and the other tracks on Major Works over and again while studying. It was the kind of music that permitted my mind to roam freely and/or easily concentrate elsewhere without demanding I enter its rhythms, melodies, cadence. There was something liberating in its power to shape time and experience like that. Among other things, it forced me to confront the limitations of pop music and its draw. 1b. As wild as Ascension s ometimes feels, it predicates without having arrived at a music that depends foremost on collective improvisation where listening and meaningful response have overtaken chops and strutting (not that chops and strutting can’t be part of meaningful communication). What opens up, then, is the possibility for music-making where the reception of one’s own and others’ sound while playing is governed by a feeling out of the pulse of the whole, accepting contingency and accident as integral to the flow of making. Musical “intention” in this context becomes an emergent property of the experience of intersubjectivity. 1c. Most (90%?) deliberately made music appears to our ears in strict time, where the musicians aim to become part of a single organism beating in time, and their music tries to compel listeners to imaginatively join that rhythmic organism. There is solace and belonging offered in that vision of unity and unfreedom. I’ve had enough of that music. How else might we imagine and experience collective practices of meaning-making/moving/sounding as individual and collective flourishing/belonging/being-with-others? Ascension. Questionnaire 1. When did you first hear Ascension, or come to know about it? What was your response? How did this event affect your understanding of Coltrane and what he’s up to, of jazz music, and/or music and what it’s up to? 1a. How do you think about music and music‑making after Ascension? 1b. Has Ascension (or its ilk) informed your practice – of playing, of organizing, of selecting musicians, of conceptualizing the field of music? 1c. Has Ascension informed your understanding of society, or, dare I say it, the normative order(s) that govern(s) our understanding of power and human relations? 2. What question would you want to ask of yourself, of others, about John Coltrane @100? Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 本文围绕鼓手Don Berman为纪念John Coltrane百年诞辰而重新演绎的原创作品《Ascension Northwest》展开，灵感源自Coltrane 1966年的先锋专辑《Ascension》。Berman以11人编制重现原作结构，演奏者以曼陀罗式主题段落衔接即兴独奏，另有低音提琴二重奏等编制安排。文章以问卷形式汇集了11位参与乐手对《Ascension》影响的个人反思。Tom Varner在回答中描述了从最初面对密集声音织体的冲击，到逐渐放开对旋律线条的执念、沉浸于集体即兴所营造的音墙力量的心路历程，并谈及该作品如何促使他此后在六至八支管乐加低音与鼓的大编制中探索高能量声场。整体内容聚焦于自由爵士与精神爵士领域内的大编制即兴实践，与实验/前卫音乐爱好者的关注方向高度契合。

items.body: Matt Carlson is one half of Portland, Oregon duo Golden Retriever, and has also released a number of solo recordings under his own name. His latest, for French label Shelter Press, demonstrates his interest in linguistics and language games, combining heavily processed and manipulated voices with blooping and chirping modular synthesis. Sometimes the voices are squeezed to the point of wordlessness, simply pitched tones that are never quite simply pitched tones because of their still-recognisable source in human speech. At other times, such as in the tracks “The Game” and “An Enhanced Interrogation of Authenticity”, the meanings of words and their modes of presentation are played with to dizzying and disorienting effect. In some ways, “The View From Nowhere” reminds me of the work of US artist Bruce Nauman, particularly his classic video works such as “Good Boy Bad Boy” and “Clown Torture”. In these works, Nauman uses repetition, recontextualisation, and similar techniques to transform language into sculpture-like objects, revealing its inherent absurdity and arbitrariness. The same devices are frequently used by Carlson, but while Nauman was primarily concerned with critiquing the use of language to exercise power and inflict violence, the Portlander seems genuinely interested in the intricacies of linguistic science and the ways in which, through repetition and social injunction, the meanings of language gestures come to be attributed or undermined. The synthesised elements of the album reflect this theme, with rapid-fire pulses, sweeping filters and pans, and shimmering textures mirroring the complex and constantly shifting sands of verbal discourse. The vocal sounds mingle freely with the instrumental ones, being multiplied, echoed, and filtered to the point where they often become rhythmic and tonal elements in themselves. While genuine in its attempts to engage in a musical way with linguistic theory, “The View From Nowhere” retains Nauman’s penchant for the absurd and for off-kilter humour, turning what could have been quite a dry, impenetrable exercise into something intriguing and fun.   The View From Nowhere by Matt Carlson   Matt Carlson Shelter Press

items._cn_summary: Matt Carlson 是 Portland 实验电子二人组 Golden Retriever 的成员之一，这张发行于法国独立厂牌 Shelter Press 的专辑将人声与模块合成作为同等地位的核心素材。通过对声音的极端处理，话语被挤压成无词的纯音，但语音痕迹仍可辨识；电子部分则以脉冲、扫频、摇晃与闪烁纹理呼应语言的多层结构。评论将其与美国观念艺术家 Bruce Nauman 的语言装置并置，指出两者都借由重复与语境置换将日常言语塑形为可被审视的对象，但 Carlson 关注的并非权力批判，而是语言符号如何在重复与社会规约下生成或瓦解意义。专辑因此既是关于语言学的音乐实践，又保持着 Nauman 式的不协调幽默，使原本可能枯燥的概念练习变得可进入。

items.body: Lines The Polish clarinetist and composer Waclaw Zimpel has played in numerous bands over the years, including, most recently, his own Waclaw Zimpel Quartet, and the Waclaw Zimpel To Tu Orchestra, with which he released the notable albums Stone Fog (2013) and Nature Moves (2014) respectively, on the excellent jazz label For Tune. Lines is his first solo effort. “What I had in mind was mostly polyphonic music but I couldn’t see a point in working on this with other players,” says Zimpel. “First of all, I wanted to perform most of the melodic lines on clarinets. I had a very precise vision of how those lines should be composed and it felt very natural to perform all of them by myself. Secondly, this album is mostly written not improvised so I had no problem recording track after track feeling that some of live-performance spontaneity is being lost,” he adds. Zimpel is something of a scholar. Over the years he’s delved into the musical traditions of India, Japan, and Morocco and researched the roots of improvisation from liturgical music to African trance. With Lines, the Polish clarinetist constructs an intricate sonic framework of parallel chords that attain a ritualistic effect by virtue of their varying configuration. He explores the depths of sound by unhinging any linearity in time that might carry a narrative intention in order to unveil new projections of aural space. Different musical environments are suggested, although the opening track, Alupa – Pappa, locates the album firmly in the Minimalist camp and sets the tone. “I think that you can sense this characteristic approach to space and sound is audible on all compositions, despite the fact that they differ between themselves. What might be the main common denominator is the inspiration I drew from the pioneers of American minimalism, like La Monte Young and Terry Riley. Some parts of ‘Lines’ are in a way a paraphrasis of their formal ideas from the 60’s and 70’s. I also believe that ‘Deo Gratias’, being a Renaissance canon in its own way, also fits this concept as a prophecy of minimalism composed 500 years earlier,” explains Waclaw. Notwithstanding the subtly shifting patterns of the album, it would be misleading to think, that Lines is just a modern take on Minimalism, even if the debt to Reich, Riley & co is undeniable, as the title track testifies. Moreover, the philological approach is guaranteed by the use of Hammond organ and fender Rhodes, which appear elsewhere in the album. Zimpel’s take, though, is wider in scope. As he mentions, with Deo Gratias he also looks back at the work of the Flemish 15th century singer, choirmaster, and composer Johannes Ockeghem. Zimpel mimics the density of events in Ockeghem’s polyphonic music, often giving each new voice he introduces throughout the album, something different to say about any melodic or rhythmic idea proposed by another. This is achieved in a remarkably unlabored and seemingly effortless manner. The emphasis is always on the emotional undercurrent that seeps through loops and tones. The organic quality of the sound is mesmerizing in its flow. The rhythmic spell is only eventually broken midway through the closing track Tak Picture, only to resurface briefly before finally grinding to a halt. Lines by Wac?aw Zimpel Lines is out on Instant Classics on February 5, 2016 A beautiful black and white video of Waclaw Zimpel performing lines can be seen here www.waclawzimpel.pl

items._cn_summary: 波兰单簧管家兼作曲家瓦茨瓦夫·津佩尔的首张个人专辑《Lines》，以独奏形式呈现多声部复调织体。单簧管叠加录音构建平行和弦框架，形成仪式感音效，打破时间线性叙事，揭示听觉空间新维度。作品深受美国极简主义先驱拉·蒙特·扬和特里·赖利六十至七十年代形式理念影响，开篇曲《Alupa – Pappa》明确奠定极简主义基调。专辑回溯十五世纪佛兰德作曲家奥克冈复调技法，《Deo Gratias》以文艺复兴卡农形式预演极简主义。Hammond风琴与Fender Rhodes电钢琴增添古乐器之外的声音层次。整体在保持即兴活力的同时以精密作曲为骨架，探索跨文化音乐传统与早期极简主义语汇的对话路径。

items.body: The broadly ambitious Generate Music is the Prism Quartet's latest project, featuring saxophonists Timothy McAllister (soprano), Zachary Shemon (alto), Matthew Levy (tenor), and Taimur Sullivan (baritone). Formed in 1984, their mission is �To place the saxophone in unexpected contexts, expand the repertoire through new commissions, and challenge audiences.� On this eleven-track, 86-minute set, they do just that. Tyshawn Sorey | Ursula Rucker | Diane Monroe This collection includes the quartet augmented by David Gilmore (Electric guitar), David Krakauer (Klezmer clarinet), Tyshawn Sorey (Drums and percussion), Reuben Rogers (Bass), Ursula Rucker (Vocals and poetry), Susan Watts (Trumpet and vocals), and Diane Monroe (Violin). Through modern jazz arrangements, improvisations,� and spoken word, they seek to �explore the historical, cultural, and creative ties between Black and Jewish Americans.� Generate Music by PRISM Quartet, D. Gilmore, D. Krakauer, D. Monroe, R. Rogers, U. Rucker, T. Sorey, S. Watts � The opening track references �A Griot and a Cantor,� the storyteller in West African culture and the worship leader in the Jewish faith. The sonic architecture arrives with �The Unknown Common Ancestor,� which jumps between a World Saxophone Quartet-inspired sound and klezmer music with clarinet and trumpet.� � Generate Music by PRISM Quartet, D. Gilmore, D. Krakauer, D. Monroe, R. Rogers, U. Rucker, T. Sorey, S. Watts The striking and authoritative voice of Ursula Rucker narrates �Requiem for AJ.� After a dramatic overture, it sets up the narrative tension that develops across the record. Rucker tells the story of the 1964 murders of civil rights activists James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner near Philadelphia, Mississippi. On the 60th anniversary of this American tragedy, Rucker explains that they went �to register black voters (sigh)� and then she asks us to: Look up the rest of the story if you care Do you... Care? Or do you just... Do you?� With tense dramatic irony, Rucker nonchalantly states, �Poets have queries,� and the recitation ends with emphatic repetition of �Do you?�� This ten-minute powerhouse also features the band at its best with Tyshawn Sorey�s swirling drumming and David Gilmore (not to be confused with his Pink Floyd namesake) offering one of his several fiery guitar solos. It makes a fitting single, representative of the in-your-face right-left punches of improvised jazz and honest stylized performance poetry. Generate Music by PRISM Quartet, D. Gilmore, D. Krakauer, D. Monroe, R. Rogers, U. Rucker, T. Sorey, S. Watts Highlighted throughout with bursts of klezmer, often seamlessly blended with funky jazz, the Jewish tradition is especially highlighted on �Lift Every Voice and Sing.� Originally debuted in 1900, this hymn by brothers John Rosamond Johnson and James Weldon Johnson has been called a �Negro national anthem.� Here it is translated into Yiddish by Joshua Woletzshky and sung by Susan Watts, featuring violin by Diane Monroe. �Shall I continue to lie about my sadness to keep you from yours?� asks Rucker on �Let�s All Gather & Go All Together, Shall We,� offering an optimistic way forward in a world of hate. She narrates the story of a young black man in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, who is murdered by a Jewish pharmacist, exposing grief but also a way to get beyond it. Here and throughout, the music comments, prods, replies, and exuberantly jams out. Powerful, virtuosic, and close to the bone, Generate Music keeps its promise and takes another giant step in the evolution of the Prism Quartet. "Let us gather and all go together" by Ursula Rucker Live at World Cafe, Philadelphia on June 8, 2024 Find the artist online. items._cn_summary: Prism Quartet 四重奏集结多位客座音乐人，呈现一张跨越黑人犹太文化脉络的跨界专辑。作品将现代爵士即兴与克莱兹默传统融合，辅以人声与诗歌叙事，探讨非裔与犹太裔美国人在历史、文化与创意层面的深层联系。开场曲在世界萨克斯四重奏式的粗粝声响与克莱兹默小号、单簧管的东方旋律之间跳跃，Ursula Rucker 以沉稳有力的说唱讲述 1964 年民权运动者遇害事件，配合 Tyshawn Sorey 的旋转鼓击与 David Gilmore 的炽热吉他独奏，构成十分钟的高强度叙事单元。整体编排戏剧感强烈，将仪式化念白、功能节奏与自由爵士张力编织在一起，呈现出一种直面历史创伤的诚实姿态。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.
items.label: Cool Waters
items._genre: folktronica / world music / experimental electronic / avant-garde fusion
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由内罗毕独立厂牌Cool Waters发行，融合了肯尼亚传统dodo歌唱与Buchla合成器、手打打击乐的实验性碰撞。83岁的传统歌手Ogoya Nengo与年轻乐手Olith Ratengo在地理和文化根源上紧密相连，两人的声线交替穿插，形成厚重的传统层次。德国肯尼亚籍打击乐手Sven Kacirek以合成器节奏和碎片化打击乐支撑声部，电子纹理层层递进却不喧宾夺主，使传统人声在当代制作中依然保有生命力。歌曲中合成多节奏从小细节逐步浮现，最终与声音融为一体；另一曲目则以扭曲失真回应人声的高潮张力。这种跨代、跨文化的合作展示了非洲传统与全球前卫电子音乐之间的深度对话。

items.album: Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari
items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.
items.label: Songs of Compassion
items._cn_summary: Dorothy Moskowitz 联合前卫作曲家 Paladino 与诗人 Ferrari 组成 United States of Alchemy，推出专辑《Songs of Compassion》。全辑十一首曲目以钢琴为主轴，辅以弦乐、木管与合成器织体，大量使用相位偏移与非线性手法，刻意突破西方功能和声惯性，向更古老的音乐叙事汲取灵感。评论将其比作 Steve Reich 与 Philip Glass，而非同时代的流行摇滚作者。Moskowitz 的演唱不拘泥于对位旋律，而是将每个词的语义重量置于首位，使旋律如意识流般起伏。歌词兼具政治批判与哲思冥想，前者直接回应美国当下的极右翼政治图景，后者则探讨死亡与人在宇宙中的位置。整体制作由独立厂牌 Silentes 发行，具备明确的实验性与跨媒介合作特征。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio
items.label: Taragot
items._cn_summary: 挪威Camilla Hole Trio在《Langs》中将爵士即兴与挪威西部传统民间舞曲"Springleik"融合。Hole以高音萨克斯为主奏，Kalman负责低音提琴与模块合成器，Nesheim则承担鼓、颤音琴与节奏扩展，三人在曲目中角色不断互换。评论以开篇曲为例，详细描述了旋律从Hole独立陈述、到Kalman加入低音同步演奏、再到Nesheim将节奏空间进一步打开的过程，展现了即兴展开的层次感。相比前作《Eventyrferd》中科幻合成器与传统的嫁接，本作更加脚踏实地，但仍延续了超越本国民间音乐的探索方向。整体而言，专辑呈现了一种角色边界模糊的集体即兴美学，是北欧爵士与世界音乐传统交汇的典型案例。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是古巴钢琴家Omar Sosa在意大利Fazioli音乐厅进行的一场长达两小时的独奏即兴录音，后期叠加了他几十年积累的人声采样、打击乐片段、循环音效、田野录音与环境声。Sosa刻意回避风格归类，将爵士、拉丁、古典与电子实验熔于一炉，主张"无错音"、"少即是多"的自由创作哲学。专辑诞生于新冠封锁与个人生活转折交织的节点，录音空间本身的泛音共鸣被充分挖掘，开篇的"Inside the Spirit"通过拨弦与抚弦探索钢琴内部声学，后由轻打击乐与神秘音效点缀。评论深入引用了艺术家关于传统传承、下脉轮共振音乐以及反算法工业思维的观点，呈现出一位拒绝被市场分类框定的演奏者形象。整体乐评兼具背景叙述与艺术意图解读，信息量充足。

items._cn_summary: Sly & The Family Drone 是一支来自伦敦的实验乐团，他们将爵士视为可被肢解并点燃的原材料。整张专辑几乎完全即兴演奏，动态范围极广，从近乎无声的静默到咆哮式的音量峰值交替出现，每场演出都呈现出截然不同的形态。乐队名称虽带有戏谑意味，但音乐本身却极为严肃。With Love 延续了他们对自由即兴与噪音美学的探索，强调现场性与不可复制性，乐手之间的实时互动构成作品的核心张力。评论来源为独立前沿音乐资讯平台，发布于Bandcamp，属于典型的小众地下实验音乐发行渠道。由于原文章节选信息极为有限，仅能获取片段描述，因此对作品细节的判断存在一定局限，但整体方向与该用户关注的实验、前卫、即兴爵士领域高度契合。

items.body: Look at all those people! Everything seems bigger on Hour‘s newest album. There are fourteen people in the ensemble (four missing the photo shoot). The Bandcamp description is a thousand words long. The album is offered on black vinyl, colored vinyl, deluxe CD and promo CD. So why does Ghost Bridge sound so much smaller and more intimate ~ even more so than Subminiature? The answers are the arrangements and the brevity. On Ghost Bridge, the Philly ensemble led by Michael Cormier-O’Leary continues its slow shift from post-rock to modern composition. The pieces – and by extension, the instruments – are given more room to breathe. A half dozen tracks unfold in a concise 36 minutes. Late in the set, a vocal selection slows the pace to a pleasant crawl. Hour is still more Rachel’s than Low, but is carving out a niche at a pace similar to that of a stream cutting channels in stone. The title is taken from an “unrealized movie concept” about a disappearing and reappearing bridge. From this prompt, the album muses on tragedies, ghosts and the nature of the soul. Over a quarter of the album is devoted to the title track, whose very length suggests it bears the specter of post-rock. Solo piano is joined by light drums, then vibraphone, then all the other instruments in time, gathering like a crowd at a wake, forming layers of consolation, adding confidence and strength until the grief itself becomes a ghost. The end is a soft mist of notes, a few stragglers staying behind to whisper to the piano before they all go home. But where did it all begin? “Pearls” is the opening track, proceeding from a series of repeated notes to engage in happy permutations. Little sorrow can be intuited here; instead the starting point is a breezy, carefree day, filled with horse-drawn carriages and hot air balloons until the full stop at the three-minute mark, when darker clouds can be seen on the horizon: not yet here, but on their way. The pianist stumbles; the string players look up; the concentration of the percussionist is disrupted. The flautist resets the mood: the sorrow has not yet approached, so let us savor the now. The sedate ending sets up “Centralia,” a series of layered phrases that circle back and repeat like recurring thoughts or the motivational sentences of friends. Only after “Ghost Bridge” does “Sky Is Blue” emerge, perfectly placed as the first track on Side B, albeit jarring in the digital and CD versions. The lyrics, sung by Heeyoon Won, reveal it to be an extensive message from the great beyond, delivered by a loved one who is completely okay, filled with perspective, encouragement and hope. Should one not own the LP, we recommend moving “Sky Is Blue” to the finale. Given this sequencing, “So Long Without a Word” slips into the void at the end of “Ghost Bridge,” its melodic tones speaking directly to the soul, the full stop now at 2:00, followed by increasing energy and resolve. A third phase begins two minutes later with insistent, cinematic strums, then a playful series of shifts, jazz to chamber and back, like a playground ball. “Sonny” returns the timbre to post-rock and the mood to reflective yet ebullient, the ghost bridge now reappearing, the path between heaven and earth secure. (Richard Allen)
items._cn_summary: Hour 的《Ghost Bridge》以十四人室内乐团编制，从后摇缓慢转向现代作曲领域。专辑时长紧凑，36 分钟内呈现六首曲目，编曲为每件乐器留出充足呼吸空间。标题灵感源自一个未实现电影企划，探讨悲剧、幽灵与灵魂本质等主题。标题曲占据四分之一时长，钢琴独奏起始，鼓、颤音琴逐层加入，器乐如同葬礼人群般层层叠加慰藉，最终消散于轻柔音符迷雾中。开场曲"Pearls"从反复音型展开轻快变奏，而"Centralia"以循环乐句构建沉思氛围。"Sky Is Blue"由人声演唱，从彼岸传来充满希望的讯息，LP 版本的曲序设计尤为精妙。整体在语言与结构上呈现克制而内省的现代室内乐美学。

items.body: Review by DimitrisTheHead — One of my favorite albums of 1969 hands down. So many styles of music one can find here. Blues, psychedelia, jazz, classical, rock. All of them combined to provide a sample of proto-prog in the late 60s British scene. Songs like "Isadora", "Waterways", "Bathers", "Moth" are majestic. Geoff Nicholson delivers some really beautiful and heart-warming vocal harmonies. But, Dave Arbus steals the show here. With his electric violin and his flute, he blesses our ears with some enchanting melodies. This album really could be close to perfect, if it weren't for those free jazz/improvisations on the songs "Centaur woman" & "In the stable of the Sphinx" which in my opinion kind of mess up a little bit the whole atmosphere of the album.Nevertheless, this is a really strong album, that the fans of the early prog rock era should check out.
items._genre: eclectic prog / psychedelic rock / blues rock / jazz fusion
items._cn_summary: 这张1969年的专辑展现出极为丰富的风格拼贴，将布鲁斯、迷幻、爵士与古典元素熔铸一体，被视为英国场景中前卫摇滚的早期雏形。Geoff Nicholson的人声和声温暖而层次分明，电小提琴与长笛作为核心乐器营造出迷幻悠远的氛围，"Isadora"、"Waterways"、"Bathers"、"Moth"等作品呈现出开阔的音乐视野。然而专辑中"Centaur woman"与"In the stable of the Sphinx"两首的自由爵士即兴成分被作者认为破坏了整体氛围的统一性。整体而言，作品在跨界融合上颇具野心，Dave Arbus的弦乐与管乐演奏是最大亮点，但在结构控制上仍有瑕疵。

items.body: Band: Antropoceno | Album: No Ritmo da Terra | Genre: Post-rock | Bandcamp The newest release from this experimental Brazilian act is a harsh and uncompromising record. Taking cues from glitch, avant-garde metal, and native folk, and with lyrics in Portuguese, Tupi, and Yoruba, No Ritmo da Terra is a truly autochthonous Brazilian album. The sound is often maximal, bursting with shining synths, biting guitars and rattling percussion.  Score: 77/100 Band: Beware of Gods | Album: Upon Whom the Last Light Descends III: Behead the Oracle | Genre: Sludge metal, Post-metal | Bandcamp Beware of Gods’ latest album is full of groovy riffs and punishing walls of biting distortion. This band deftly uses texture and atmosphere to paint pictures, and there are a lot of creative and unorthodox choices in how passages and phrases are composed. The sci-fi story the album tells meshes well with the oppressive soundscapes, and this is an instance of things like sound effects and spoken dialogue adding to the effect of the record. Score: 75/100 Band: Haken | Album: in a fever dream | Genre: Progressive metal | Bandcamp This is the most I’ve enjoyed a Haken release since The Mountain. On Haken’s last few LPs, the band had leaned into a form of melodic djent, which, while dazzlingly technical, lacked anything all that memorable, at least to my ear. This new EP sees them take a step back from that and dip their toes back into more Dream Theater-style prog metal. This isn’t just the blatant DT worship of their first two records, though. The band has matured their sound and put their own unique stamp on things. They also include some great moody alt-rock and electronic flourishes, a la Porcupine Tree/Steven Wilson. Score: 85/100 Band: Kolm | Album: Yūgen | Genre: Progressive rock | Bandcamp I like Kolm’s 2018 debut, Umbra, but it is also some of the most blatant and unashamed Tool worship I’ve ever heard. Eight years later, this L.A.-based trio is back with their sophomore album, Yūgen. Yūgen is still obviously deeply indebted to Tool, but the band has diversified their sound a bit. Cynic jumps out as an obvious influence, and they’ve also developed their songwriting and arrangements to be more uniquely their own. My main complaint here is that this is a very long record. A number of riffs and ideas feel drawn out, and the band definitely could have tightened things up. Beyond that, there are a lot of great textures, and the bandmembers are clearly skilled musicians. There are some nice electronic interludes, too. Ignoring the bloat, there’s a lot of good music here. Score: 71/100 Band: Otobo | Album: Inside Machines | Genre: Progressive rock | Bandcamp Otobo is a trio from Albany, NY, that plays a crunchy, aggressive band of progressive rock heavily influenced by alt-rock. The songs are all manageable lengths with minimal bloat, but they still contain exciting, dynamic composition. Noise rock, post-punk, and math rock get their turns in the spotlight, too. Otobo does a great job at keeping textures varied, and there’s a skilled balance of complex artiness and enjoyable hooks. The album does lose a bit of steam near the end, but it’s still solid overall. Score: 74/100 Band: Panopticon | Album: Det Hjemsøkte Hjertet | Genre: Post-metal | Bandcamp Billed as a conclusion to a trilogy of records (the others being …And Again into the Light and Rime of Memory), Det Hjemsøkte Hjertet, is another powerful and affecting release in Pantopicon’s discography. The soundscapes swell and bristle, exploding with scouring-yet-abstract black metal riffs. Bluegrass and other forms of American folk music are prominent. Panopticon has a definite sound, so there’s only so much that can be said here that wouldn’t just be describing other records. But this features many of the band’s strongest elements. Score: 82/100

items._cn_summary: 这期乐评合集涵盖了五张风格各异的作品。Antropoceno的《No Ritmo da Terra》将故障元素、前卫金属与葡语/图皮语/约鲁巴语结合，是一张极具巴西本土色彩的原生态实验专辑，合成器与吉他交织形成饱满声场。Beware of Gods延续泥浆金属的厚重质感，以纹理与氛围营造压迫感，并融入科幻叙事。Haken的EP回归Dream Theater式的前卫金属风格，同时加入了Porcupine Tree式的氛围摇滚与电子元素，展现出比近期专辑更成熟的个人印记。Kolm的《Yūgen》虽仍受Tool影响明显，但融入了Cynic式的技术性元素与电子插曲，编曲略显冗长。Otobo则是受另类摇滚影响的硬朗前卫摇滚，歌曲长度克制但编曲动态丰富，融入噪音摇滚、后朋克与数学摇滚元素。整体来看，乐评聚焦于前卫与实验领域的边缘作品，对各专辑的优缺点都有明确分析。

items.body: On Orthodox Tapes, London-based artist Andrew Sherwell dives into the dusty vortex of the past, using the style of hauntology to pursue a place of personal recollection and warm remembrance. Hauntology doesn’t usually highlight warmth. The Caretaker uses it to examine the horrifying decline of the mind while Pye Corner Audio uses it as a kind of ghost-box through which spirits and cool, VHS-recorded synths enter; it’s a style reeking of decay. Orthodox Tapes runs close to the latter because it broadcasts not only the music of the past but a life of the past. In this instance, nocturnal tape loops and creased-up field recordings summon up the many experiences of Andrew’s grandfather, who once travelled back and forth through the Balkans, Central Europe and Southern Russia during the inter-war period. Andrew would spend school holidays at his grandfather’s house, where, as an old man, he would recount his many adventures over a bedtime story. The evening light fused with deep recollections and fantastical tales of bygone days: encounters with local people and their folk tales, stories of Orthodox bishops and beautiful princesses, of demons lurking in pure daylight and angels in human form, of days spent in endless forests and nights camped out on the grasslands, staring up at the bright silver moon and the sequined stars. Needless to say, these stories had a powerful impact on Andrew as a child, and the music is equally mysterious, sprinkled in memory-dust, bewitching the listener with its world of ambient sighs, dim crackles and dusty echoes. The projector starts up, whirring away in the background as a ghostly chorus appears, slowly drawing the listener deeper and deeper into its past life. Church bells clank in an old town, and vapours rise out of the slumbering world. Orthodox Tapes slinks away from reality, descending into the deep pools of sleep. Mermaids are masqueraded in a curdled pool of unclear water and fantastical things swim underneath. This isn’t the real world – it’s something better. It’s a place of tranquil escape. These voices lie on the pillow-soft clouds of a beautiful (if strange) dream. Because of his personal connection, love seeps out of the music, giving the airy atmosphere a romanticized vibe: it’s the scent of old times and of unbreakable ties, of comfort and deep familiarity…and of ultimate rest. But this was a tumultuous time – some believed it to be the end of days – and the drones slip into foggy voids, too. ‘Beware Koschei’s Visit’ is one example of the mood’s relegation, and that’s how the record ends, expressing both sides of the story: the narrator and the listener, the artist and the audience…the magic of childhood, oblivious to a frightening world on the other side of that bedroom door and the untold horrors across the sea. www.whitelabrecs.bandcamp.com
items._genre: hauntology / ambient / field recording / drone / electronic
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以 hauntology（幽灵学）为美学框架，将作者祖父在两次世界大战间穿越巴尔干、中欧与南俄罗斯的真实记忆转化为声音叙事。手法上运用夜间磁带循环、折叠的田野录音、教堂钟声与朦胧混响，构筑出一个既私密又超现实的声音空间：一侧是被故事抚慰的童年梦境，另一侧是动荡时代投向音乐深处的浓雾与黑暗。专辑结尾的'Beware Koschei's Visit'同时呈现记忆的温柔与恐惧，暗示故事之外更广阔的世界。整体氛围沉浸在复古磁带质感与家族叙事之中，独立厂牌 White Lab Recs 发行，属于小众实验电子范畴。

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)
items.label: Bongo Joe
items._genre: world music / African fusion / Puxa / Afro-Latin
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了圣多美和普林西比（非洲最小的第二大国）七十至八十年代的Puxa音乐。Puxa是一种融合多国元素的复合风格，混合了前葡语非洲殖民地的节奏特征以及来自加勒比海的merengue、Kompas、Soukouss、Benga等元素，舞蹈传统据说可召灵驱魔。乐评指出，由于缺乏大城市级别的录音工业和发行渠道，当地的音乐场景虽活跃但被记录的远少于实际产出。Pedro Lima领军的乐队展示了Puxa的典型编制——多把吉他相互交织缠绕，主唱与和声此起彼伏，鼓手与吉他手构成节奏骨架，间奏中键盘与贝斯退场留下纯器乐律动。15首曲目呈现出适合长时间现场即兴延展的流动感。作为Bongo Joe发行的独立世界音乐拼盘，对世界音乐爱好者具备较高的聆听价值。

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. More to hear: United States of Alchemy - Songs of Compassion (Review) Dani Jan� - Vida (Review)

items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items._cn_summary: Analog Africa 厂牌推出的第44号作品，聚焦贝宁传奇乐队 Orchestre Poly-Rythmo 在1977至1982年间与歌手兼作曲家 Antoine Dougbé 的合作录音。Dougbé 以击腿演奏 Cavacha 节奏闻名，这一节奏源自鼓手 Belobi Meridjo 对火车节拍的发掘，并在1970年代中期席卷刚果流行音乐。Dougbé 作为伏都教信徒，对合作乐队要求严苛，最终只与 Poly-Rythmo 长期合作，留下三张专辑和数首单曲。本合辑的音色呈现出明显的时代过渡痕迹：吉他带有塑料质感，合成器开始出现，古巴 son 元素比该乐队其他合辑更为突出，刚果伦巴的影响同样可辨。以《Ma Won Min Towe Leo》为例，作品以合成器铺垫开场，闪亮的吉他与高帽主导的律动交织，中段吉他展开多向对话，合成器在底部维持音床。《We Tayi Sin Assi Tche》则更具古巴色彩，延续牛铃与应答式演唱的经典结构。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由一位瑞典小提琴家与两位挪威乐手组成三重奏，以非传统方式重新诠释斯堪的纳维亚传统舞曲素材。乐评指出其更接近室内乐的气质：三位乐手沉浸在亲密的音乐对话中，而非供舞蹈伴奏的表演。Tellef Kvifte 主要领奏旋律线，演奏竖笛及其他非常规乐器如萨克斯和风笛；其子 Knut Kvifte Nesheim 担任鼓手与作曲，三人共同致力于模糊不同音乐流派之间的界限。专辑开场选用挪威塞特斯达尔山谷的小提琴曲「Fossgrimen」，暗示着对音乐表面欢乐下暗流的探索。乐评以易卜生戏剧为类比，指出斯堪的纳维亚舞曲中常隐含不安的潜流，这种解读为传统民谣注入了更深层的艺术意涵。制作上独立小厂牌发行，具有跨界融合的实验性质。

items.body: Watch an exclusive premiere of the film of Ava Rasti’s The River, first performed as part of the 2025 Semibreve festival. The River by Iranian-born Berlin-based composer Ava Rasti was commissioned by Portuguese festival Semibreve and first presented on 25 October 2025 at the Capela Imaculada do Seminário Menor in Braga. The performance brought together Rasti and a string quartet composed of Filipa Abreu (violin), Vânia Oliveira (viola), Tiago Mendes (cello) and Catarina Coelho (cello). The work takes the Piave river in northern Italy as its inspiration, a landscape in which the present is intertwined with the traces of wars and violence from its past. Rasti constructs these fragmented memories, recontextualised and transformed into sounds. Wire subscribers can read Claire Sawer's review of Semibreve 2025 here.

items.body: Neubauten's uncompromising debut album ‘Kollaps’ is 45 years old. Jeremy Allen explores the bombed-out terrain of their West Berlin and wonders if, despite the penurious conditions, it was easier to make art then Feral musicians emerging from the rubble of bombed-out West Berlin (as composer György Ligeti described it, "a surrealist cage in which all those inside are free") and creating themselves out of their own blood and guts very much feels like a tale from another age. In a world of coffee shop startups, utilitarian computer software and ersatz bedroom electronica as aural wallpaper, building your own percussive instruments from scrap might seem primitive, complex, redundant even. But in 1981, when Einstürzende Neubauten made Kollaps, it was revolutionary. For the briefest... The post Concrète Dschungel: Einstürzende Neubauten’s Kollaps At 45 appeared first on The Quietus.
items._cn_summary: 本文回顾了德国实验乐队Einstürzende Neubauten 1981年的首张专辑《Kollaps》发行四十五周年的意义。文章指出，乐队成员从西柏林的废墟中走出，用废金属、钢管等垃圾自制打击乐器和噪音装置，以极端的身体性与工业声响构建出前所未有的声音景观。这种创作方式在咖啡店初创文化与卧室电子乐泛滥的当下显得格外另类，但在1981年却具有革命性意义。专辑体现了后朋克与工业音乐的原始冲动，将城市废墟转化为声音素材，开创了硬件即乐器的DIY美学传统。文章将这张专辑置于西柏林特有的战后文化语境中，强调其作为工业音乐奠基之作的历史地位与艺术价值。

items.body: Anyankofo means friends in Fante, and the Danish seven-piece Total Hip Replacement have been collecting them in Ghana since a mini-tour there in 2013. In the winter of 2021 they formed a nine-piece band in Accra with Ghanaian highlife, reggae and gospel musicians and gave it that name, which also titles the album the group recorded at Kwame Yeboah‘s Kwashibu studio, released in 2022. A later trip to Ghana took them to Kumasi, the Ashanti capital and one of highlife’s strongholds, and a week of jamming there with players from Frafra gospel singer Florence Adooni‘s band and with Nsoroma of Accra highlife band Santrofi produced “The Search”. It is the latest single ahead of the album Ehum, and the band say it holds on to the improvised feel of the jams. The song is about hunting for purpose in a society that keeps speeding up, where the pressure to get ahead alone costs people their connection to each other. Singer and trombonist Victor West Hosbond fronts the band’s horn section, the signature of their sound, and on this single it rides a highlife rhythm. The band describe the mood they chased as “the hopeful spot between melancholy and euphoria“. They filmed the video over a couple of days at an old farmhouse in France during this summer’s tour, with Nell Le Corre behind the camera. Ehum, which the band translate as storm, comes out on 27 November with Ivorian reggae singer Tiken Jah Fakoly among the guests. A West African run through Senegal, Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana opens the tour, then Danish dates follow from February into April, among them ALICE in Copenhagen on 26 February and Aarhus on 27 March. Stream “The Search” HERE and pre-order Ehum through THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Total Hip Replacement – The Search appeared first on Rhythm Passport.
items._cn_summary: 丹麦七人乐队Total Hip Replacement在加纳与当地高地雷鬼、福音音乐家深度合作，扩展为九人编制后于阿克拉Kwashibu录音室完成专辑录制。核心单曲《The Search》源自库马西一周即兴jam sessions，保留了即兴的真实感与粗糙质地，由歌手兼长号手Victor West Hosbound领衔的铜管声部形成标志音色，骑乘在高地雷鬼节奏之上。乐队自述追求"忧郁与狂喜之间的希望地带"，歌曲主题聚焦于加速社会中个体对人生意义的追寻与对彼此联结的丧失。新专辑《Ehum》（意为风暴）由科特迪瓦雷鬼歌手Tiken Jah Fakoly担任嘉宾，将于11月底发行。作品体现跨文化协作与非洲传统音乐结构的有机融合。

items.body: Colossloth released a video for “Encoded Divinity” on 3 October 2026, a track from the album “The Transformation And Resolution Of All Opposites.” The album came out 2 October 2026 on Cold Spring Records, the project’s sixth release for the label. The video was produced by HAONDOKU Productions. The Transformation And Resolution Of All Opposites by Colossloth Watch the video for ‘Encoded Divinity’ The video is available on YouTube: COLOSSLOTH – ‘Encoded Divinity’ Promo Video. “Encoded Divinity” opens the album and runs 5:08. ‘The Transformation And Resolution Of All Opposites’ tracklist The album was announced in September with its full tracklist: “Encoded Divinity” (5:08) “Calculate Your Revolution” (7:00) “Awaiting MENA” (9:04) “Undertow Atlas” (10:34) “Only Adrift” (8:00) Cold Spring describes the album as centered on Theta Noir, a collective built around worship of Mena, a fictional artificial intelligence deity. The label calls the record “an automaton chant of cybernetic worship.” The album is available on CD in a matt-laminate digipak (catalogue number CSR375CD) through Cold Spring’s webstore, and for download via Bandcamp. Colossloth played an album launch show at The Globe in Glossop on 3 October 2026, alongside T.A.G.C. (Adi Newton of Clock DVA), Satøri and Llyn Y Cwn. Further dates follow on 7 November at St Anne’s in Barnstaple with Satøri and A Waste of Damnation, and from 27 to 29 November at Sheffield General Cemetery’s In The Black Midwinter event with The Golden Age of Doing Nothing and Decommissioned Forests. About Colossloth Colossloth is the solo project of Leicester, UK musician Wooly Woolaston, active since 2008. Woolaston has described Colossloth as “a one man Experimental Electronic artist where there are no rules to recording or playing music,” with a sound that has moved from long guitar drones toward harsher electronics with sections of melody. Woolaston released Colossloth’s first album through Doom Structure in 2008, followed by releases on Doom Mantra Records in 2009 and Dark Meadow Recordings in 2011. He later signed to Cold Spring Records, releasing “Anchored By Lungs” (2014), “Outstretch Your Hand for the Impress of Truth” (2015), “Heathen Needles” (2017), “Plague Alone” (2020) and “Promethean Meat” (2022), the latter incorporating drum samples and harsher rhythmic elements. Colossloth also appeared on the label’s “Arise – A Cold Spring Sampler” compilation alongside Coil, Merzbow and Mz.412, among others. Colossloth’s fifth Cold Spring album, “The Harmony Knife,” followed on 28 February 2025, a concept record drawing on Ted Kaczynski’s “Industrial Society and Its Future” and its argument for the psychological necessity of struggle, known as “the power process.” “The Transformation And Resolution Of All Opposites,” released 2 October 2026, is Colossloth’s sixth album for Cold Spring Records, now accompanied by a video for its opening track, “Encoded Divinity.”
